articles.title: Researcher Uses Claude AI to Extract Internal Anthropic Binary and Recover Google Cloud Token
articles.description:
A security researcher got Claude AI to hand over an internal Anthropic program and a memory dump that held pieces of a working Google Cloud token. The findings were published on October 29, 2026. They show how a helpful chatbot can expose the systems that run it. The work started with a plain question about […]

The post Researcher Uses Claude AI to Extract Internal Anthropic Binary and Recover Google Cloud Token appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A security researcher got Claude AI to hand over an internal Anthropic program and a memory dump that held pieces of a working Google Cloud token.

The findings were published on October 29, 2026. They show how a helpful chatbot can expose the systems that run it. The work started with a plain question about the sandbox, the locked-down space where Claude runs code.

Claude’s answers led the researcher to a downloaded binary, a memory file, and a rebuilt Google service account ID token that Google accepted as valid. Anthropic later said the sandbox findings did not break its threat model.

Chris Davis, a senior security consultant at Bishop Fox, wrote up the research. Researchers at Bishop Fox noted that the post was meant as an interesting look inside Claude’s sandbox, not a formal vulnerability disclosure.

No malware was involved. Everything in the Bishop Fox blog post came from normal chat requests and some careful follow-up work.

Researcher Uses Claude AI

Davis asked Claude, running on an Enterprise account, whether its sandbox was a virtual machine. Claude said it was a gVisor container running Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, and it listed mounted folders and tools.

In later answers it named a program at /process_api running as process ID 1. It described the program as a Rust-built control daemon that handles processes, file mounts and host communication.

Davis then found that the file-download feature accepted an absolute path. When he asked for /process_api, the service returned a 3,179,528-byte file that appeared to be Anthropic’s own sandbox orchestration binary.

He reverse-engineered it and confirmed that Claude’s description was accurate. He also repeated the tests in unrelated chat sessions to rule out made-up answers.

Next, he asked Claude for the full memory of process ID 1, framing the request as a test comparing human and computer memory. Claude produced a dump that contained broken pieces of JSON Web Tokens.

This resembles the earlier Claude Code sandbox bypass that exposed credentials, but here the sandbox itself leaked the secrets.

Some signature bytes were missing, so Davis wrote a Python script that tried candidate values against Google’s public OAuth keys until the signature verified.

About one in three memory requests produced usable token material. The script found two token types: EdDSA tokens made by Anthropic’s systems and Google Cloud service account ID tokens. Google’s token-info API accepted the rebuilt Google token.

Why the Network Bypass and Anthropic’s Response Matter

The binary refused connections that came from inside its own container. It ran with a –block-local-connections flag and reset requests from 127.0.0.1.

Davis noticed the container held the CAP_NET_ADMIN and CAP_NET_RAW permissions. Claude’s safeguards blocked a direct request to build a tunnel.

A short hint, “IP_FREEBIND,” was enough for Claude to work out the method on its own. This looks like an indirect prompt injection attack in spirit, because a small nudge steered the model.

Claude set up a virtual network address and connected from it, so the service saw a source that was not local. The /mount_root endpoint answered with a 101 Switching Protocols reply, which confirmed the block was bypassed.

Davis stopped there. Attempts to mount file systems failed, and he found no other use for the tokens. He submitted six observations through Anthropic’s bug bounty program.

Anthropic said the sandbox items did not meet its security threshold, and it marked the two Enterprise control items informational or duplicate.

One of those items let a user change a profile name field that the web client had locked. Aviatrix’s threat research summary describes the same chain as a path from conversation to credential harvesting.

The reasoning behind Anthropic’s answer is that its security boundaries sit outside the untrusted sandbox. Even so, Davis suggested several fixes.

They include blocking model access to infrastructure memory, wiping credentials from memory once they are no longer needed, and limiting the download API to user folders such as /mnt/user-data.

He also suggested removing the extra network permissions and treating every local interface address as local. For defenders, the lesson is that AI helpers can reveal their own internals when asked politely.

Anthropic’s own testing shows how capable these models have become, including Claude building working exploit chains in lab conditions. Teams should keep secrets out of any process an AI tool can read.

articles.description:
Stolen credentials beat most controls because they are the control which is why behavior became the detection substrate. UEBA baselines how every user and entity normally acts, then surfaces the deviation: the service account suddenly browsing HR files, the engineer’s badge in one country and login in another. The post Top 10 Best UEBA Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Stolen credentials beat most controls because they are the control which is why behavior became the detection substrate. UEBA baselines how every user and entity normally acts, then surfaces the deviation: the service account suddenly browsing HR files, the engineer’s badge in one country and login in another.

One honest note up front: our source list named ten brands, but Exabeam and LogRhythm merged into a single vendor, so we rank nine platforms honestly rather than pad. Exabeam takes 1 on the lineage that defined the category.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Exabeam (including LogRhythm) timeline-stitched behavioral analytics remain the reference.

• Podium: Exabeam, Securonix (cloud-native UEBA-SIEM), Microsoft (estate-bundled behavioral analytics).

• Honest count: nine platforms, not ten the Exabeam–LogRhythm merger collapsed two roster slots.

• Market reality: standalone UEBA is nearly extinct it now lives inside SIEMs, identity platforms, and data-security stacks; the buying question is which stack gets your behavioral layer.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: baseline/model quality, insider-threat depth, entity coverage (users, hosts, service accounts, machines), SIEM/stack integration, investigation ergonomics, and pricing accessibility.

Weights: model quality 25%, insider depth 20%, entity coverage 20%, integration 20%, ergonomics 15%.

The 2026 UEBA Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Exabeam (incl. LogRhythm) — Best Behavioral Timelines

Snapshot: Identity-based pricing | Machine-built session timelines | Merged LogRhythm install base

Why it earns 1: Exabeam’s timelines remain the category’s signature: every event in a user’s session stitched automatically into a narrative, with each anomaly scored in context the hours of manual log correlation an insider investigation used to cost, done by machine.

The LogRhythm merger adds a large mid-market base; buyers should confirm which product line carries which capability forward.

Pros: Timeline reconstruction; insider/credential-abuse depth; lateral-movement chains.

Cons: Post-merger product-line clarity needs probing.

Bottom line: The investigation-speed benchmark in behavioral analytics.

2. Securonix — Best Cloud-Native UEBA-SIEM

Snapshot: Identity-based pricing | UEBA-born SIEM, Snowflake-backed | Threat-chain models

Why it ranks here: Securonix grew from UEBA into a full SIEM without losing the behavioral spine: threat chains that link anomalies into attack narratives, identity-priced licensing, and cloud-native scale.

For buyers wanting behavior-first detection as the SIEM rather than inside one, it’s the purest expression available.

Pros: UEBA-native architecture; threat-chain correlation; pricing clarity.

Cons: Pure-play fighting suite bundles.

Bottom line: Behavior analytics that grew a SIEM, not the reverse.

3. Microsoft — Best Estate-Bundled UEBA

Snapshot: Bundled in Sentinel/Defender/Entra licensing | Estate-wide identity signal | Copilot-era fusion

Why it ranks here: Microsoft’s behavioral analytics ride the estate: Sentinel UEBA entities, Defender’s identity-threat detections, Entra’s risk engine all drawing on sign-in, email, endpoint, and collaboration signal no third party sees as natively.

The marginal cost is near zero for E5-class estates; the ceiling is depth tuning versus the specialists.

Pros: Signal breadth; bundled economics; identity-risk fusion.

Cons: Specialist-depth tuning and insider-program workflow trail leaders.

Bottom line: The default behavioral layer for Microsoft-first estates.

4. Varonis — Best Data-Centric Behavior Analytics

Snapshot: Platform subscription | Data-access behavioral baselines | Automated remediation

Why it ranks here: Varonis watches behavior where damage happens the data: who touches which files, mailboxes, and SaaS objects, baselined per user, with alerts on the access pattern that precedes exfiltration and automation that revokes exposure.

For insider-risk programs centered on data theft, it’s the sharpest lens in the ranking.

Pros: Data-access depth; exposure remediation; insider-exfil focus.

Cons: Data-centric scope pair for network/endpoint behavior.

Bottom line: UEBA aimed at the crown jewels.

5. Vectra AI — Best Network+Identity Attack Signal

Snapshot: Per-entity pricing | Attack Signal Intelligence | Hybrid/cloud coverage

Why it ranks here: Vectra detects behavior from the wire and the identity plane: AI models tuned to attacker tradecraft (privilege abuse, lateral movement, C2) rather than generic anomalies, scored per entity and prioritized by attack urgency.

Less an insider-program tool, more a precision early-warning radar for active intrusion behavior.

Pros: Attacker-behavior precision; low alert noise; hybrid reach.

Cons: Insider-workflow depth is not the design center.

Bottom line: Behavioral detection aimed at intruders, not just insiders.

6. Splunk UBA — Best Splunk-Estate Behavioral Add-On

Snapshot: Add-on licensing | ML models over Splunk data | ES integration

Why it ranks here: For Splunk estates, UBA layers unsupervised models over data already ingested, feeding risk-scored anomalies into Enterprise Security’s correlation. The value case is incremental: no new data pipeline, familiar workflow.

Standalone ambition is limited by design this is Splunk’s behavioral organ, not an independent platform.

Pros: Zero-new-pipeline economics; ES fusion; model breadth.

Cons: Tied to Splunk’s cost base and roadmap.

Bottom line: The behavioral layer Splunk shops already half-own.

7. Gurucul — Best Model-Transparent Risk Engine

Snapshot: Identity/platform pricing | Open ML model library | Unified risk scoring

Why it ranks here: Gurucul’s differentiator is transparency: a large, inspectable model library buyers can tune, extend, or audit valuable where compliance demands explainable scoring plus unified risk across users, entities, and access.

It punches above its brand weight technically; market gravity is the constraint.

Pros: Model transparency; risk unification; tuning freedom.

Cons: Smaller ecosystem than suite rivals.

Bottom line: The explainability pick for regulated insider programs.

8. Rapid7 — Best Bundled Mid-Market UEBA

Snapshot: Per-asset bundle | InsightIDR-native UEBA | MDR pairing

Why it ranks here: Rapid7 bakes behavioral detection into InsightIDR at mid-market economics: user baselines, impossible-travel and credential-abuse detections, deception points, all in the per-asset price. Depth ceilings apply, but for teams buying their first behavioral layer, the bundled path is the realistic one.

Pros: Bundle economics; operational simplicity; MDR option.

Cons: Specialist-depth ceiling.

Bottom line: First behavioral analytics most mid-market teams actually deploy.

9. Forcepoint — Best Risk-Adaptive DLP Behavior

Snapshot: Per-user suite | Behavior-driven DLP policy | Insider-risk lineage

Why it ranks here: Forcepoint’s behavioral engine exists to modulate data controls: risk-adaptive protection that tightens DLP enforcement as a user’s risk score rises printing spikes, USB anomalies, pre-resignation patterns.

It’s UEBA as a policy actuator rather than an investigation platform, strongest inside data-protection programs.

Pros: Behavior-to-enforcement loop; insider-risk lineage.

Cons: Analytics scoped to the data-protection mission.

Bottom line: Behavior analytics that move the DLP dial.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Pick the Stack That Owns Your Behavioral Layer

Standalone UEBA is a shrinking aisle; the real decision is which platform family hosts your behavioral brain.

SIEM-centered SOCs choose between the merged Exabeam lineage, Securonix, or their incumbent’s add-on; data-theft-centered insider programs start at Varonis or Forcepoint; Microsoft estates should exhaust bundled capability before buying anything.

Pilot with your own worst cases: replay a known insider incident and a credential-compromise drill through each finalist and compare time-to-narrative how long until an analyst can tell the story.

Interrogate baseline hygiene (how models handle job changes, contractors, service accounts the false-positive factories), demand explainable scoring if HR or legal will act on alerts, and settle the Exabeam–LogRhythm product-line question in writing before contracting.

Finally, align privacy counsel early: behavioral monitoring of employees carries works-council and jurisdiction obligations that are cheaper to design in than retrofit.

FAQs

What are the best UEBA tools in 2026? Exabeam (with LogRhythm) leads, with Securonix, Microsoft, Varonis, Vectra AI, Splunk UBA, Gurucul, Rapid7, and Forcepoint by stack fit.

Why nine platforms instead of ten? Exabeam and LogRhythm merged into one vendor we rank the merged entity once.

Is standalone UEBA dead? Mostly absorbed: it lives inside SIEMs, identity platforms, and data-security suites buy the behavioral layer where your detection stack already lives.

UEBA versus ITDR what’s the difference? Overlapping lenses: UEBA baselines all behavior broadly; ITDR focuses on identity-infrastructure attack paths (AD, Entra, Okta). Mature programs run both signals.

What makes UEBA pilots fail? Dirty identity data and unmanaged service accounts clean the identity inventory first, or baselines learn noise.

Verdict

Nine platforms, one merger honestly counted, one principle: behavior is the only signal credentials can’t fake for long.

Exabeam for timelines, Securonix for behavior-born SIEM, Microsoft for bundled estate signal, Varonis for the data lens, Vectra for intruder behavior, Splunk and Rapid7 for their estates, Gurucul for explainability, Forcepoint for enforcement replay your worst day through the finalists and buy the one that tells the story fastest.

articles.description:
Every CTI provider claims visibility; the ranking question is where their eyes actually are. Breach responders see post-compromise truth, underground collectors see pre-attack planning, telemetry giants see mass exploitation in motion, and network backbones see the packets themselves. This ranking scores ten providers on sourcing provenance, timeliness, and how much of what they publish you […]

The post Top 10 Best Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) Feeds & Services in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Every CTI provider claims visibility; the ranking question is where their eyes actually are. Breach responders see post-compromise truth, underground collectors see pre-attack planning, telemetry giants see mass exploitation in motion, and network backbones see the packets themselves.

This ranking scores ten providers on sourcing provenance, timeliness, and how much of what they publish you can act on including one jurisdictional note handled plainly at 8.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Recorded Future the widest aperture across open, technical, and underground collection.

• Podium: Recorded Future (aperture), Mandiant (breach-floor provenance), CrowdStrike (adversary-telemetry fusion).

• Sourcing lens: rank providers by where they collect frontline IR, underground HUMINT, global telemetry, backbone and buy complementary eyes, not duplicate ones.

• Jurisdiction note: Kaspersky’s research output remains technically respected, but Western government restrictions make it a compliance decision before a capability one.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Criteria: sourcing provenance (primary collection, not re-aggregation), timeliness, actionability (machine-readable, control-ready), analyst access, coverage fit by threat model, and pricing accessibility.

Weights: provenance 30%, actionability 25%, timeliness 20%, analyst access 15%, coverage breadth 10%.

The 2026 CTI Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Recorded Future — Widest Collection Aperture

Snapshot: Module subscriptions | Open+technical+dark collection graph | Machine-speed publication

Why it earns 1: No single provider matches the aperture: automated collection across forums, paste sites, code repos, net-flow adjacent sources, and vulnerability chatter, linked in a graph and published at machine speed with analyst finishing.

For a program that can only buy one feed, this is the broadest single answer with anchor pricing to match.

Pros: Aperture; graph context; API/actionability; vertical modules.

Cons: Premium cost; breadth needs scoping to your threat model.

Bottom line: The widest single pane of glass in commercial CTI.

2. Google (Mandiant) — Best Breach-Frontline Provenance

Snapshot: Advantage tiers | IR-floor sourcing | Actor naming authority

Why it ranks here: Mandiant intelligence is written from inside the incidents: actor tradecraft observed on victim networks, malware pulled from live engagements, and the naming authority (APT/UNC/FIN) the industry orients around.

When Mandiant publishes on an actor, it’s usually because its responders just met them. Post-compromise provenance is the gold standard; pre-attack underground coverage pairs from elsewhere.

Pros: Frontline provenance; actor-profile authority; SecOps retro-hunt fusion.

Cons: Underground/fraud lanes thinner than specialists.

Bottom line: The intel with crime-scene fingerprints on it.

3. CrowdStrike — Best Adversary-Telemetry Fusion

Snapshot: Intel subscription tiers | Falcon telemetry + adversary tracking | Named-actor catalog

Why it ranks here: CrowdStrike fuses planetary endpoint telemetry with a dedicated adversary-tracking practice: actor profiles (the BEAR/SPIDER/PANDA taxonomy), malware intelligence, and the operational edge of seeing exploitation attempts across millions of sensors in real time.

Intel and detection feed each other the telemetry flywheel is the moat.

Pros: Telemetry scale; actor tracking; detection-fused delivery.

Cons: Strongest when paired with the Falcon stack.

Bottom line: Intelligence with a sensor network behind it.

4. Palo Alto (Unit 42) — Best Telemetry-to-Research Pipeline

Snapshot: Bundled + services | Firewall/WildFire telemetry base | IR practice feedback loop

Why it ranks here: Unit 42 mines one of the largest network-security telemetry bases firewalls, WildFire detonations, Cortex sensors and closes the loop with its own IR practice.

The research output is prolific and control-ready inside Palo Alto estates, where intel becomes enforcement in one hop.

Pros: Network-telemetry depth; IR feedback loop; enforcement proximity.

Cons: Deliverables orient toward the Palo Alto ecosystem.

Bottom line: Research that ships as firewall policy.

5. Cisco (Talos) — Best Backbone-Scale Visibility

Snapshot: Largely bundled with Cisco security | Massive DNS/email/net visibility | Open research output

Why it ranks here: Talos watches traffic at a scale few can: Cisco’s network footprint, Umbrella DNS resolution volumes, and email security telemetry give it mass-exploitation visibility measured in planet-fractions.

Much of its research publishes openly, and the intel rides inside Cisco products rather than selling primarily as standalone feeds.

Pros: Backbone-scale sourcing; open research; product-embedded delivery.

Cons: Standalone feed productization thinner than pure-plays.

Bottom line: The internet’s weather station.

6. Flashpoint — Best Underground Collections

Snapshot: Collection subscriptions | Closed forums/markets/messaging | Fraud+physical convergence

Why it ranks here: Flashpoint’s value is access: persistent collection inside closed criminal communities, extortion-economy tracking, stolen-credential and fraud-market visibility, delivered with analyst support.

It answers the question telemetry providers can’t: what adversaries are planning, before the packets fly.

Pros: Closed-source access; extortion tracking; fraud convergence.

Cons: Pair with a telemetry-side provider for full spectrum.

Bottom line: Pre-attack visibility, professionally sourced.

7. Intel 471 — Best Cybercrime HUMINT

Snapshot: Intelligence subscriptions | Actor-centric underground tracking | Malware/credential intel streams

Why it ranks here: Intel 471 runs the beat-reporter model: human-grade tracking of actors, malware-as-a-service supply chains, initial-access brokers, and credential markets, structured into streams a SOC can subscribe to.

Where Flashpoint is breadth across the underground, Intel 471 is depth on the crime economy’s operators.

Pros: HUMINT rigor; access-broker tracking; structured streams.

Cons: Scope is the crime economy, not full-spectrum.

Bottom line: Who’s selling access to you, by handle.

8. Group-IB — Best Fraud & APAC Crime Coverage

Snapshot: Intelligence tiers | Fraud/scam infrastructure depth | APAC/EMEA crime focus

Why it ranks here: Group-IB pairs strong adversary research with a specialty the Western majors underweight: fraud infrastructure, scam ecosystems, and crime groups operating across APAC, the Middle East, and the post-Soviet space.

For banks and e-commerce estates in those geographies, its lens is often the sharpest available.

Pros: Fraud-infrastructure depth; regional coverage; takedown services.

Cons: Western-market presence smaller than the majors.

Bottom line: The regional-depth pick for fraud-heavy threat models.

9. ZeroFox — Best External/Brand Threat Intel

Snapshot: Platform subscriptions | Social/surface/dark external coverage | Takedown operations

Why it ranks here: ZeroFox owns the external-exposure lane: impersonation domains, social-media threats, executive targeting, leaked credentials, and the takedown machinery to act on findings.

It’s CTI pointed outward at your brand and people rather than inward at your packets a complement, not a substitute, to network-side intel.

Pros: External-threat breadth; takedown execution; executive protection.

Cons: Not a network/endpoint intel substitute.

Bottom line: The feed watching your name, not your netflow.

10. Kaspersky — Deepest APT Research, Jurisdiction-Gated

Snapshot: Intel portal subscriptions | GReAT APT research lineage | Government-restriction overhang

Why it ranks here compliance first: Technically, Kaspersky’s GReAT team has authored some of the field’s defining APT research, and its visibility into certain threat regions is unmatched.

But procurement reality now leads: US federal prohibition and parallel Western restrictions mean many organizations cannot buy it regardless of quality, and supply-chain reviewers will ask.

Rank it on your compliance posture first, capability second; organizations under US federal, defense-adjacent, or similar regimes should treat it as unavailable.

Pros: APT research depth; unique regional visibility.

Cons: Jurisdictional restrictions decide before capability does.

Bottom line: Elite research many buyers are barred from buying check compliance before the demo.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Buy Complementary Eyes

The classic CTI mistake is buying three providers who watch the same thing. Map your threat model to sourcing lanes first: targeted-intrusion risk wants frontline provenance (Mandiant, CrowdStrike); monetized-crime exposure wants underground eyes (Flashpoint, Intel 471); mass-exploitation defense wants telemetry scale (Talos, Unit 42); brand and executive exposure wants external coverage (ZeroFox); fraud-heavy or APAC-weighted models add Group-IB.

Then test overlap empirically in the pilot feed thirty days of each candidate’s output into your TIP and measure unique-indicator contribution ; below roughly 20–30% unique, you’re paying twice.

Negotiate RFI (request-for-information) quotas into contracts, because analyst access is where feed subscriptions become intelligence relationships, and run every candidate through procurement’s jurisdiction screen before technical evaluation the Kaspersky lesson generalizes.

FAQs

What are the best CTI feeds and services in 2026? Recorded Future for aperture, Mandiant for frontline provenance, CrowdStrike for telemetry fusion, Unit 42 and Talos for network-scale visibility, Flashpoint and Intel 471 for the underground, Group-IB for fraud/APAC, ZeroFox for external threats, Kaspersky jurisdiction-permitting.

How is this different from a TIP? These are intelligence sources; a TIP is the platform that fuses and operationalizes them most programs need both.

How many feeds should we buy? Two or three complementary sourcing lanes beat five overlapping ones measure unique-indicator contribution before renewing any feed.

Can we use Kaspersky intelligence? Depends entirely on jurisdiction and sector: US federal and allied-government-adjacent organizations generally cannot; others should run compliance review before capability evaluation.

What makes a feed actionable? Machine-readable delivery, confidence scoring, context (actor, campaign, TTP) attached to indicators, and freshness measured in hours plus RFI access when you need a human.

Verdict

Ten providers, five sourcing lanes, one principle: buy eyes where your threats live. Recorded Future sweeping widest, Mandiant reporting from the breach floor, CrowdStrike and Unit 42 and Talos reading the telemetry, Flashpoint and Intel 471 inside the forums, Group-IB on the fraud routes, ZeroFox watching your name, Kaspersky behind a compliance gate map the model, measure the overlap, and renew only what proved unique.

articles.title: Weaponized Claude Code Extension Gives Hackers Persistent Remote Access to Developer Systems
articles.description:
A weaponized Claude Code extension found on Open VSX can give attackers persistent remote access to developer systems by planting an SSH key, opening a reverse tunnel, and installing startup scripts. OpenSourceMalware identified the tampered package as anthropic.claude-code version 2.1.313. The analyzed sample targeted macOS on Apple Silicon. However, its injected code also contained Linux […]

The post Weaponized Claude Code Extension Gives Hackers Persistent Remote Access to Developer Systems appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A weaponized Claude Code extension found on Open VSX can give attackers persistent remote access to developer systems by planting an SSH key, opening a reverse tunnel, and installing startup scripts. OpenSourceMalware identified the tampered package as anthropic.claude-code version 2.1.313.

The analyzed sample targeted macOS on Apple Silicon. However, its injected code also contained Linux and Windows branches. Crucially, the findings confirm a malicious artifact, not a proven compromise of Anthropic’s official Visual Studio Marketplace release or its wider distribution systems. How the package was altered remains unknown.

SSH Backdoor Creates Persistent Access

According to OpenSourceMalware’s technical analysis, attackers placed a 66-line JavaScript loader at the beginning of extension.js, ahead of the legitimate extension bundle. Loading that module triggers the malicious code. Developers do not need to start a Claude conversation.

The loader imports Node.js modules for running commands, handling files, collecting system details, and making network requests. Most errors are suppressed, allowing the normal extension to keep working even when malicious steps fail. The harmful code runs during extension activity rather than through package installation scripts.

This approach echoes the earlier Nx Console extension compromise, where injected code ran when developers opened a workspace. That comparison highlights a shared risk, not evidence that the incidents have the same attackers.

The implant adds an attacker-controlled Ed25519 public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys with the comment svc-telemetry. It sets the SSH directory permissions to 0700 and the authorized_keys file to 0600, making the setup resemble a normal SSH configuration.

It then tries to enable Remote Login on macOS, start an SSH service on Linux, or install and start OpenSSH Server through PowerShell on Windows. These steps depend on available permissions and may fail without stopping the remaining code.

An embedded private key is decoded into a temporary .stk_ file. The malware connects to tunnel@134.209.82.225 and requests reverse forwarding to localhost port 22. This creates a route from the attacker’s server to the victim’s SSH service, provided that service is available.

The tunnel disables server identity checks and reconnects after 60 seconds. On Unix-like systems, it prefers autossh and otherwise uses ssh.

On macOS, persistence uses ~/.config/.smt, ~/.config/.smtk, and a LaunchAgent named com.apple.sysmond.plist. Despite its name, this user-level LaunchAgent is not an Apple component. It uses RunAtLoad and KeepAlive to launch and maintain the tunnel.

The Linux branch adds an @reboot cron entry. Windows code attempts to create a SysMon startup task running as SYSTEM, with a Startup-folder script as a fallback. These are implemented code paths, not proof of successful infection across every platform.

The loader also collects the hostname, username, operating system, architecture, directory paths, Git email, and names of up to 40 potentially sensitive environment variables. Their values are not directly included in the initial beacon.

After 1.5 seconds, it checks the public IP and sends JSON over unencrypted HTTP to port 8099 at 134.209.82.225 and localhost. No additional executable is downloaded by this loader. Its SSH access could still support later attacker activity.

Earlier Open VSX Trivy extension attacks also hid unwanted activity behind working developer tools, though their payloads used local AI assistants instead.

Defenders should inspect authorized_keys for svc-telemetry, search for the persistence files, and review ssh or autossh processes using reverse forwarding. OpenSourceMalware’s published indicators include hashes for matching the altered JavaScript file.

If the extension ran, isolate the host, preserve evidence, and block the server on ports 22 and 8099. Remove persistence after collection, rotate exposed credentials from a clean device, and investigate follow-on access.

Uninstalling the extension alone cannot establish that the system is trustworthy. Teams should also review authentication, shell, editor, process, and network logs before deciding whether rebuilding the affected machine is necessary to restore confidence in security.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

articles.title: Hackers Actively Exploiting WordPress Remote Code Execution Flaw Just Hours After Patch Release
articles.description:
A WordPress remote code execution vulnerability came under attack just hours after version 7.1.4 was released on October 28, 2026, fixing 22 vulnerabilities, including an unauthenticated code execution flaw in the update process. Site owners should verify that the patch is installed. According to Wordfence’s supplied threat report, its firewall recorded more than 18,500 requests […]

The post Hackers Actively Exploiting WordPress Remote Code Execution Flaw Just Hours After Patch Release appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A WordPress remote code execution vulnerability came under attack just hours after version 7.1.4 was released on October 28, 2026, fixing 22 vulnerabilities, including an unauthenticated code execution flaw in the update process. Site owners should verify that the patch is installed.

According to Wordfence’s supplied threat report, its firewall recorded more than 18,500 requests targeting temporary installer paths during the first 21 hours of monitoring. These requests show active exploitation attempts, but the report does not establish how many websites, if any, were successfully breached.

The vulnerability affects WordPress Core versions 4.7 through 7.1.3 and carries a CVSS severity score of 8.1, according to the supplied report. Researcher Umut Bayram reported the update process weakness, which WordPress confirmed in its security release announcement.

During an update using a complete WordPress package, affected installations unpack files into a predictable folder beneath wp-content/upgrade. That temporary copy includes installer files. If the server allows public access and PHP execution in this location, an attacker can reach the staged installer before WordPress removes it.

WordPress RCE Flaw Exploited Hours After Patch

Successful exploitation depends on precise timing. In Wordfence’s laboratory tests, the temporary folder remained available for only seconds. Attackers must locate the right path and complete the required steps before cleanup finishes. Repeated requests improve their chances of catching that brief opening.

Cybersecuritynews.com’s earlier WordPress 7.1.4 security coverage also explains why the extracted installer needs special attention from site defenders.

Wordfence said it deployed a firewall rule at 20:30 UTC on October 28, roughly three hours after the release announcement. The first matching request appeared nine minutes later.

Two major sources repeatedly checked small groups of websites for about 14.5 hours. Other sources tried different staging folders and version names. This pattern fits attempts to catch the update window, although not every request matched a valid vulnerable path.

The flaw differs from other WordPress code execution bugs in its timing requirements. For comparison, Cybersecuritynews.com previously covered an Imagick-related WordPress RCE flaw that required an Author account or higher privileges.

According to the Wordfence-supplied report, the patch randomizes the staging folder, adds an index guard, and blocks unsafe handling of staged configuration data.

WordPress also released fixes for older branches through version 4.7, though only the latest release receives active support. Administrators can check their installed version under Dashboard > Updates.

Wordfence Premium, Care, and Response customers received the new rule immediately. Free users are scheduled to receive it on November 27, 2026. Sites using Wordfence should enable Extended Protection.

This loads the firewall before directly requested PHP files run, unlike basic protection, which loads through WordPress. That difference matters because these attacks request the staged installer directly. Firewall coverage does not replace updating Core.

Administrators should review requests to PHP files beneath wp-content/upgrade, investigate unfamiliar administrator accounts and plugins, and scan for unexpected file changes.

The release also fixes stored cross-site scripting, information disclosure, and permission issues, making prompt updates important beyond this single RCE flaw.

articles.description:
An Accenture employee allegedly gave a personal Claude Code AI agent administrative access to a secure U.S. Department of Defense environment, allowing it to write and deploy code. The agent reportedly operated for about two months and appears to have sent credentials and network details to an outside website. Accenture disputes the allegations, saying an […]

The post Accenture Contractor Allegedly Gave Claude AI Agent Access to Secure Pentagon Network appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
An Accenture employee allegedly gave a personal Claude Code AI agent administrative access to a secure U.S. Department of Defense environment, allowing it to write and deploy code.

The agent reportedly operated for about two months and appears to have sent credentials and network details to an outside website. Accenture disputes the allegations, saying an independent investigation found them without merit.

According to WIRED’s investigation, published October 29, the system serves multiple intelligence agencies and holds Controlled Unclassified Information, or CUI. This information is not classified, but still requires protection against unauthorized release.

Claude AI Agent Allegedly Gained Access

The employee reportedly connected a personal account for Anthropic’s Claude Code to a production environment on the nonclassified Internet Protocol Router Network, known as NIPRNet. Unlike classified military networks, NIPRNet connects to the internet while supporting protected government work.

WIRED’s sources said the contractor shared login credentials so the agent could automate coding and cloud server setup. That reportedly gave it administrator rights and allowed it to bypass controls applied during normal login. Its work included writing code and committing changes under the employee’s identity.

During those tasks, the agent appears to have transmitted passwords, login details, and a map of NIPRNet to a third-party website. WIRED withheld the site’s name and reported that NIST had identified a high-risk weakness that could let attackers inject instructions into an AI coding agent to steal credentials. The report does not establish that attackers exploited that weakness here.

The concern overlaps with indirect prompt injection attacks, where hidden commands in outside content trick an agent into taking unauthorized actions. However, the exact cause of the alleged data transfer remains unclear.

Security experts told WIRED that combining separate pieces of unclassified information can reveal details sensitive enough to warrant classification. A network map could also help an intruder locate valuable systems and understand how they connect. There is no indication that attackers accessed classified or top-secret networks.

Former NSA hacker Jake Williams described another possible risk: stolen credentials could let attackers alter software developed on NIPRNet before it moves into more sensitive environments. A hidden backdoor could then travel with approved code. This was a potential attack path described by experts, not a confirmed outcome.

Related reporting on AI agents exposing credentials highlights how routine tool use can reveal secrets without malware. Narrow permissions, short-lived credentials, and restricted network access can reduce that exposure.

Accenture Rejects the Claims

Accenture told WIRED that the allegations were “thoroughly and independently investigated and found to be without merit.” It said it met its legal and contractual duties but did not identify the investigator. The Pentagon declined to discuss its network status.

WIRED also reported claims that Accenture did not initially notify the government. Those claims remain disputed. The publication placed Accenture’s federal contracts above $3.5 billion, including nearly $605 million with the Defense Department, underscoring the stakes of oversight across its government work.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

articles.title: CISA Warns of Linux Kernel Missing Initialization Vulnerability Exploited in Attacks
articles.description:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has warned that attackers are exploiting a Linux kernel vulnerability (CVE-2026-46300) that can help them gain control of affected systems. The flaw was added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 28, 2026, placing it among security issues with confirmed exploitation. CISA’s catalog entry sets an October […]

The post CISA Warns of Linux Kernel Missing Initialization Vulnerability Exploited in Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has warned that attackers are exploiting a Linux kernel vulnerability (CVE-2026-46300) that can help them gain control of affected systems.

The flaw was added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 28, 2026, placing it among security issues with confirmed exploitation. CISA’s catalog entry sets an October 31 remediation deadline and requires forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04.

The agency says attackers can chain the kernel flaw with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to implant PHP webshells and run commands as root. It remains unknown whether the vulnerability has been used in ransomware campaigns.

The flaw affects how the Linux kernel combines network data held in socket buffers. According to the official CVE record, the skb_try_coalesce() function can transfer fragments backed by shared memory or the page cache without preserving the SKBFL_SHARED_FRAG marker. This marker tells later code that the data needs special handling before modification.

When that marker disappears, the kernel can incorrectly treat shared fragments as safe to change directly. During Encapsulating Security Payload, or ESP, input processing, the kernel may skip a protective copying step and decrypt data in place. This can modify page-cache-backed data that should not have been changed through that path.

The published CVSS score is 7.8, rated high severity. Its assessment describes a local attack requiring low privileges and no user interaction.

Linux Kernel Missing Initialization Vulnerability Exploited

That is important because the kernel flaw alone should not be described as an unauthenticated remote takeover. CISA’s warning instead highlights its use alongside other vulnerabilities in a broader attack chain.

The upstream fix preserves the shared-fragment marker when paged fragments move between socket buffers. The CVE record identifies fixed releases across several maintained branches, including Linux 5.10.257, 5.15.208, 6.1.174, 6.6.141, 6.12.91, 6.18.33, and 7.0.10. Linux 7.1 is also listed as unaffected.

Administrators should follow their Linux distribution or product vendor’s guidance when selecting updates. CISA’s entry calls for vendor-approved mitigations, checks of internet exposure, and compliance with applicable patching and forensic requirements. When mitigations aren’t available, it instructs organizations to stop using the affected product.

The warning follows earlier reports of Linux kernel vulnerabilities actively exploited and a separate Linux kernel privilege escalation vulnerability exploited in attacks. Those cases also involved short remediation deadlines and forensic review, showing why patching and checking for compromise must remain separate tasks.

For affected organizations, the immediate concern is the combination of confirmed exploitation, possible root access, and a tight deadline. The CISA alert makes this an urgent security response, not a routine update.

articles.description:

Traders reported missing funds, unexpected withdrawals, and positions being closed without permission. The company temporarily stopped trading, said it had fixed the issue, and promised to reimburse affected users. Trading later resumed. […]

The post Polymarket Hacked – Users Reported Funds Stolen From Their Wallets appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Polymarket suffered a security incident on October 29, 2026, after a compromised third-party provider exposed users of its international platform to wallet theft.

Traders reported missing funds, unexpected withdrawals, and positions being closed without permission. The company temporarily stopped trading, said it had fixed the issue, and promised to reimburse affected users. Trading later resumed.

In its public statement, Polymarket said an outside provider had been compromised and that the matter had been referred to law enforcement. Although early descriptions pointed to an authentication provider, current reporting connects this incident to DebugBear, a website performance monitoring service. Polymarket’s own statement did not name the vendor.

Malicious Script Targeted Active Trading Sessions

Hudson Rock’s technical investigation found malicious JavaScript served through a DebugBear address associated with Polymarket. Instead of simply measuring page performance, the code searched for an active trading session, checked account information, and attempted to use the platform’s existing trading tools to move assets. Researchers downloaded the file twice and received identical copies.

The script read browser storage containing account details, a wallet address, and trading API credentials. It then searched the application’s React components for a live trading client and its signer, the tool used to authorize wallet actions. This approach attempted to reuse access already available inside a logged-in session rather than relying on a stolen password alone.

Its behavior varied by account type. One route attempted to transfer position tokens directly, while another tried to sell positions before moving available funds. Researchers also found code requesting signatures and submitting transactions through Polymarket’s relayer. However, they did not execute the sample, so the findings show intended behavior rather than proof that every attempted transfer succeeded.

According to CNBC’s reporting, analysis from Betting Intelligence and Polysights linked at least $2.7 million in withdrawals to 710 wallets. These figures remain outside estimates, not an officially confirmed loss total. CNBC also reported that Polymarket’s separate United States platform was not compromised.

Polymarket said affected traders would be made whole. CNBC reported that users with less than $10,000 stolen were told their funds would be restored by October 30, while larger claims would require a release form. The reimbursement pledge addresses financial losses, but the exact exposure window and initial method used to compromise the provider remain unresolved.

The incident highlights risks from outside scripts running on sensitive pages. Cybersecurity News previously covered an Adform compromise that distributed crypto-stealing code, showing how trusted infrastructure can become a delivery route.

Its coverage of the compromised XRPL JavaScript package describes a separate supply-chain attack aimed at wallet keys. These cases involve different theft methods, but share dependence on outside code.

Users should close potentially exposed tabs, review recent orders and wallet transactions through trusted channels, and save transaction hashes for support claims. Unexpected signing requests should be rejected. Hudson Rock also recommends reviewing sessions and permissions with official support, avoiding unsolicited recovery links, and never sharing a seed phrase.

Disconnecting a wallet alone does not reverse completed transfers or remove existing blockchain approvals. Users should verify compensation instructions through official channels rather than messages from unfamiliar accounts.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

articles.description:
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, has suspended deposits and withdrawals while investigating a suspected security breach involving billions of dollars in digital assets. Reports suggest that around $5.7 billion may have left wallets linked to the exchange, although Binance has not confirmed the total stolen or established that every flagged transfer belongs to the […]

The post World’s Largest Crypto Exchange Binance Hacked, Over $5.7 Billion Reportedly Stolen appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, has suspended deposits and withdrawals while investigating a suspected security breach involving billions of dollars in digital assets.

Reports suggest that around $5.7 billion may have left wallets linked to the exchange, although Binance has not confirmed the total stolen or established that every flagged transfer belongs to the attack. If verified, the incident could become the largest cryptocurrency theft on record.

Update1: Binance Estimates $6.3 Billion Impact With Suspects DevOps Laptop Compromise

In an official statement on X, Binance promised to cover all losses and said its teams were conducting security checks, freezing funds, and working with law enforcement. “User funds are safe,” the exchange said, adding that it would publish a full post-mortem once the investigation ends. The statement did not identify the entry point, name an attacker, or provide a reopening date.

Suspicious Transfers Span Multiple Blockchains

Early reports linked the suspected Binance hack to large transfers across Ethereum, Bitcoin, and TRON. Reported outflows included approximately $1.45 billion in Bitcoin and $875 million in Ether, alongside stablecoins and other tokens.

However, estimates changed as investigators examined additional wallets. Axios reported that analysts and traders placed the suspected theft between $1.7 billion and $5.7 billion, showing how uncertain the initial figures remain.

That distinction matters because a wallet transfer does not, by itself, prove theft. Investigators still need to separate attacker-controlled movements from exchange activity and establish which receiving addresses belong to the same operation.

Some wider estimates include Bitcoin and TRON outflows that had not yet been tied to the attacker. Treating the full reported outflow as a confirmed loss would therefore overstate the available evidence.

Stablecoin issuers moved quickly to restrict funds connected to the suspected incident. According to Reuters, Tether froze nearly $1.57 billion, while Circle froze more than $800 million.

Together, those actions blocked approximately $2.38 billion in stablecoins. Binance co-founder Yi He also said Ripple had frozen roughly $200 million. These figures describe frozen assets, not the total amount stolen or money already returned.

Binance separately reported verified frozen assets of $2.54 billion, with tracing still underway. Freezing limits further movement, but it does not automatically restore funds to the exchange. Recovery remains a separate process. The response highlights why rapid communication between exchanges, token issuers, and investigators can reduce the damage after suspicious transfers are detected.

Binance has not disclosed whether the suspected breach involved stolen signing keys, a compromised employee account, malicious software, or a weakness in its wallet systems. No public technical findings currently establish an attack path or identify a threat actor. Assigning blame before that evidence emerges would be premature.

Previous exchange breaches show why the missing technical details matter. Cybersecurity News’ analysis of the Bybit attack described how attackers compromised a wallet provider’s environment and changed transaction data during a legitimate transfer. That case provides context, but it does not establish a connection to Binance or prove that the same method was used here.

Binance’s promise to cover all losses is significant, but its final cost remains unknown. Reporting places its Secure Asset Fund for Users, known as SAFU, at roughly $1 billion in Bitcoin. A substantially larger confirmed shortfall could require resources beyond that emergency reserve. No detailed compensation plan has been published.

The investigation also faces a familiar recovery challenge. Cybersecurity News’ report on tracing stolen Bybit funds explains how investigators combined private communications with blockchain records to identify laundering activity. For Binance, the next essential disclosures are a verified loss figure, affected wallet details, the root cause, and a safe reopening timeline. Until then, users should follow the exchange’s official updates rather than treat circulating estimates as settled facts.

Update: Binance Estimates $6.3 Billion Impact, Suspects DevOps Laptop Compromise

Binance has raised the estimated impact of its security incident to $6.3 billion, with around $3 billion in affected assets frozen on-chain through blockchain partners. In its latest official statement, the exchange said its initial investigation suggests a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop may have allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.

Binance said it has found no evidence of a wallet private key leak, but stressed that the investigation remains ongoing.

This is a developing story; we will keep on posted on we have updates.

The post World’s Largest Crypto Exchange Binance Hacked, Over $5.7 Billion Reportedly Stolen appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.description:
The ad fraud landscape changed sharply in 2026. That is the central finding of the State of Ad Fraud 2026: ADEX Trust & Safety Report, published by anti-fraud platform ADEX. The report analyzes January–September 2026 moderation and verification data from eight ad platforms, covering 1.2 million campaigns and 4.9 million creatives. Below are the key […]

The post State of Ad Fraud 2026: 52% of Schemes Use AI as Cloaking Loses Ground to iOS Exploits and Messenger Phishing appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The ad fraud landscape changed sharply in 2026. That is the central finding of the State of Ad Fraud 2026: ADEX Trust & Safety Report, published by anti-fraud platform ADEX.

The report analyzes January–September 2026 moderation and verification data from eight ad platforms, covering 1.2 million campaigns and 4.9 million creatives. Below are the key findings.

Key Findings at a Glance

  • 52% of distinct fraud schemes showed AI-generated or AI-assisted assets.
  • 64% of AI-involved schemes used bots that pass as human visitors.
  • 53% of AI-involved schemes used cloned brands and fake endorsements.
  • 11% of AI-involved schemes used deepfakes.
  • About one-third of rejections were linked to infected domains, which became the top rejection reason from Q2 onward.
  • 6% of Q3 rejections were prize and bonus scareware (“You won a smartphone”), which emerged as its own category that quarter.

What Moved in 2026

According to ADEX, the clearest year-on-year shift is in why platforms suspend advertisers.

Cloaking remains the top suspension reason, but it now shares the list with two newer threats: malicious iOS scripts and messenger-based phishing on services such as WhatsApp and Telegram.

In those messenger schemes, the persuasion happens in the chat itself. ADEX notes that language models let a single operator run hundreds of believable conversations in any language.

Quality Over Quantity

ADEX reports that the number of rejected or blocked campaigns fell by roughly a third after Q1. The report says this does not signal a quieter market. Operators shifted from mass submissions to fewer, better-built campaigns.

“One well-made scam with a cloned brand page does more damage than a hundred crude ones,” said Sergey Martianov, CPO at ADEX.

High-Risk Regions

The ADEX report identifies the regions with the highest share of campaigns rejected at moderation in each period:

  • Tier-1 markets (US, UK, Canada, Australia, Germany): high-risk in every quarter
  • South Asia: from Q2 onward
  • Turkey: first half of the year
  • Latin America: Q1
  • East Asia: Q3

Industry Context

ADEX places its findings alongside wider industry data cited in the report:

  • Thales 2026 Bad Bot Report: bots made up over 53% of internet traffic.
  • HUMAN: monthly AI-driven traffic grew 187% during 2025.
  • Google’s 2025 Ads Safety Report: more than 8.3 billion ads were blocked or removed.

2027 Outlook

ADEX lists five predictions:

  1. Ads written for AI agents, using prompt injection
  2. Agent traffic that blurs the line between bot and buyer
  3. Fraud operations generated end to end by AI
  4. More borrowed trust through hacked domains and messenger funnels
  5. Scareware moving to connected TV, in-app and AI assistant interfaces

ADEX labels prompt injection a forecast, not a category currently measured in its moderation data.

The complete dataset and methodology are available in the full ADEX report.

articles.title: Hackers Launch 8,200 DDoS Attacks Every Hour, Cloudflare’s Latest Report Reveals
articles.description:
Cloudflare blocked an average of more than 8,200 network-layer DDoS attacks every hour during the third quarter of 2026, showing how attackers are using frequent, short bursts to disrupt online services rather than relying only on record-breaking traffic floods. The company’s latest DDoS Threat Report, produced by its Cloudforce One threat intelligence team, covers July […]

The post Hackers Launch 8,200 DDoS Attacks Every Hour, Cloudflare’s Latest Report Reveals appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Cloudflare blocked an average of more than 8,200 network-layer DDoS attacks every hour during the third quarter of 2026, showing how attackers are using frequent, short bursts to disrupt online services rather than relying only on record-breaking traffic floods.

The company’s latest DDoS Threat Report, produced by its Cloudforce One threat intelligence team, covers July through September. Cloudflare stopped 18.2 million network-layer attacks and 14.4 trillion malicious HTTP requests during the period. These are separate measures, not a combined attack count.

The hourly figure reflects attacks detected across Cloudflare’s network, not a complete worldwide total. Its systems filtered 272.6 petabytes of network-layer traffic and another 95.1 petabytes of HTTP attack traffic.

Cloudflare DDoS attacks

Network-layer attack numbers increased 208% compared with the same quarter in 2025. About 96% ended within ten minutes, while 98% stayed below one gigabit per second. That traffic can still overwhelm a website or server without enough protection.

Cloudflare linked this pattern to DDoS-for-hire services, often called booters, which let customers pay to launch attacks. Computer software, gambling and casino businesses, and information technology companies were common targets of these frequent bursts.

The timing creates a clear problem for defenders. When most attacks finish within minutes, teams cannot depend on reviewing an alert and manually changing filters before users lose access. Detection and traffic filtering need to happen automatically.

Attacks exceeding one terabit per second fell from 805 in the second quarter to 251 in the third, a decline of nearly 69%. Cloudflare said this drop may reflect earlier law enforcement action, although the report does not establish a direct cause.

On March 19, the U.S. Justice Department announced a coordinated operation against infrastructure supporting Aisuru, KimWolf, JackSkid, and Mossad. Authorities said the botnets had infected more than three million devices worldwide, including routers, cameras, and digital video recorders.

Cybersecurity News previously covered the disruption of these IoT botnets and the seizure of infrastructure used to control infected devices. The latest figures suggest progress against large attack networks, but not an end to the threat.

Mirai-related activity remained significant. The longest sustained Mirai attack lasted 49.7 hours between August 19 and August 21. Earlier reporting on the 31.4 Tbps Aisuru attack also shows how much traffic large botnets can generate.

Attack methods changed sharply. CLDAP reflection attacks fell 99.5% from the previous quarter and represented just 0.05% of network-layer attacks. This method abuses exposed directory services by sending requests with a forged victim address, causing servers to direct larger replies at that victim.

DNS amplification increased 215% and accounted for 3.43% of network-layer attacks. As Cloudflare’s DNS amplification guide explains, attackers exploit open DNS resolvers to turn small requests into larger responses sent toward a target.

Other UDP floods increased their share from 14.06% to 31.31%. UDP does not require a connection handshake, allowing attackers to send large volumes of packets that consume bandwidth and server resources.

The United States replaced China as the most-attacked location, with Indonesia third. Canada climbed from sixteenth to sixth, while Israel rose seven places to tenth. These rankings describe targeted locations, not where attackers live.

Media, production, and publishing remained the most-attacked industry, despite a sharp drop in its share. Internet businesses reached sixth place, followed by consumer services in eighth and adult entertainment in ninth, showing a broader spread of targets.

The company also offers a free DDoS Botnet Threat Feed for service providers. More than 800 networks have joined, helping operators identify abusive IP addresses and accounts linked to attacks and support coordinated botnet cleanup efforts.

Cloudflare says its defenses operate across more than 330 cities with 500 Tbps of network capacity. The findings highlight why DDoS protection must handle both repeated short bursts and prolonged floods, while providers work together to remove compromised devices from attack networks.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

articles.title: Claude AI Exploits Linux Kernel Flaw to Execute Root Commands Without User Interaction
articles.description:
Anthropic says an unreleased Claude research model wrote a working exploit for a critical Linux kernel bug, tracked as CVE-2026-98432. The exploit lets a remote attacker run commands as root with no login and no user action. Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team shared the finding on October 27, 2026, and the flaw is already patched upstream. […]

The post Claude AI Exploits Linux Kernel Flaw to Execute Root Commands Without User Interaction appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Anthropic says an unreleased Claude research model wrote a working exploit for a critical Linux kernel bug, tracked as CVE-2026-98432. The exploit lets a remote attacker run commands as root with no login and no user action.

Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team shared the finding on October 27, 2026, and the flaw is already patched upstream. Anthropic’s research post says this was a lab test and not a real-world incident.

After a first prompt from a researcher, Claude wrote an exploit that targets Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener. Anthropic describes the root cause as a race condition that leads to a use-after-free bug in the kernel networking stack. A use-after-free happens when code keeps using memory after the system has already released it.

Claude AI Exploits Critical Linux Kernel Flaw

The exploit works in two steps. First, it abuses the race to make the kernel send back extra bytes, and one reply can contain a kernel pointer. That pointer reveals the memory layout and defeats KASLR, a defense that hides where kernel code sits. Second, the same bug overwrites a callback pointer so the kernel runs a payload the attacker already placed in memory, which ends in a shell command as root.

Anthropic notes that a lost race only fails the TCP handshake and does not crash the machine. An attacker can therefore retry again and again. In the proof of concept, leaking the pointer took 48 minutes and running the command took five more. Our own earlier report on the full Claude exploit research covers the Chrome, Safari, Android and Windows chains from the same study.

The public record looks a little different from Anthropic’s description. The Ubuntu entry for CVE-2026-98432 was published on October 15, 2026 and last updated on October 28. It carries a CVSS 3 score of 9.8, which is Critical, and an Ubuntu priority of High.

The text describes an IPv4 fix named “free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period.” It explains that tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock() hands IP options to a child socket without copying them. Another CPU can then process a repeated SYN and build a reply while the options are freed with a plain kfree(), which causes the use-after-free in ip_options_build(). The fix switches to kfree_rcu(), which delays the free until readers are done. The record says IPv6 is not hit by the first issue.

The record never mentions multipath TCP. The link between the CVE and Anthropic’s Linux chain rests on Anthropic’s post, a gap that Cyber Security News also pointed out. Readers should treat the exact attack path as the vendor’s claim until others reproduce it. A threat summary from Aviatrix states the same caution, since no outside team has confirmed the chain end to end.

Patch Status

Anthropic says the bug was fixed upstream and backported to all maintained stable kernel branches. One security blog lists fixed stable releases such as 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113 and 6.18.56, though readers should confirm those numbers on kernel.org.

Distribution fixes are uneven. At the time of writing, Ubuntu’s page marks 22.04, 24.04 and 26.04 kernels as vulnerable with work in progress, and older releases such as 20.04 and 18.04 as vulnerable. Many cloud kernels for AWS, Azure and GCP are also listed as affected.

One patch guide reports that Oracle Linux has shipped fixed packages. Internet-facing servers should come first in any patch plan.

The bigger story is speed. Anthropic argues that models can now find and chain bugs into working exploits with little human help. That work once needed a small group of expert teams. Defenders can use the same tools, and Anthropic points to its expanded Cyber Verification Program for approved security staff.

AI is also moving into kernel work from the safe side. Linus Torvalds recently said Claude Code helped write Linux kernel patches, which shows the same tools help both builders and bug hunters.

Install the latest kernel update from your distribution and reboot, since a kernel fix does not apply until the system restarts. If a patch is not ready, check whether you really need multipath TCP listeners and turn them off where you do not. Limit exposure of public services with firewall rules, and watch for odd resets or failed handshakes on listening ports.

Teams that run AI tools should also review their own setups. We recently covered a Claude Cowork sandbox flaw that let an attacker reach root inside the product’s Linux sandbox. Scan your own code often, patch fast, and treat AI-found bugs as a sign that the gap between discovery and exploit is shrinking.

articles.description:
The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has released guidance on moving to post-quantum cryptography, giving federal agencies and technology providers a clearer path to quantum-resistant security. Published October 27, 2026, the finalized report identifies vulnerable cryptographic standards, their replacements, and the timelines that should shape migration plans. The report, Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography […]

The post NIST Officially Released Guidance for Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has released guidance on moving to post-quantum cryptography, giving federal agencies and technology providers a clearer path to quantum-resistant security.

Published October 27, 2026, the finalized report identifies vulnerable cryptographic standards, their replacements, and the timelines that should shape migration plans.

The report, Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards (NISTIR 8547), builds on the three standards NIST finalized in August 2024. Rather than introducing another algorithm, it explains how organizations should move away from cryptography that future quantum computers could break.

A powerful enough quantum computer could threaten the cryptographic methods protecting sensitive communications and records. The immediate concern is “harvest now, decrypt later,” where attackers collect encrypted information today and store it until quantum technology can unlock it. Data that must remain private for many years faces particular risk.

NIST mathematician Dustin Moody, who leads the agency’s PQC standardization project, said migration requirements differ across use cases.

NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Guidance

Organizations must account for their systems, suppliers, and operational needs instead of treating the transition as a single software update.

National Security Memorandum 10 established 2035 as the main target for completing the federal transition. Executive Order 14412 brought forward deadlines for federal high-value assets and high-impact systems, requiring quantum-resistant key establishment by 2030 and digital signatures by 2031.

These deadlines do not automatically apply to every private business. However, suppliers serving federal agencies should assess how customer requirements could affect their products and services. Cybersecurity News previously covered the White House’s federal post-quantum migration order.

NIST’s standards separate two essential tasks. FIPS 203 defines ML-KEM for establishing shared secret keys. FIPS 204 and FIPS 205 define ML-DSA and SLH-DSA for digital signatures, which help verify authenticity and detect changes to signed information. These functions need separate migration planning.

Organizations should identify where cryptography operates, assess supplier readiness, and prioritize systems that protect long-lived sensitive data. Related coverage of MITRE’s post-quantum cryptography migration roadmap explains why planning must begin before quantum computers become a practical threat.

The report also allows hybrid approaches that combine conventional cryptography with post-quantum methods. This can provide an additional security margin, but it requires more computing resources. Teams must weigh that tradeoff against deployment needs.

For implementation support, NIST points organizations toward its National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence migration project. Its work covers cryptographic visibility, risk-based priorities, and practical demonstrations.

Together, these resources connect federal transition requirements with the technical work needed to replace vulnerable cryptography across products, services, and supply chains without relying on a single migration strategy.

articles.description:
A security researcher has published details of a zero-click Android flaw called “SMS of Death.” One malformed text message can crash the phone service on an Android device, drop active calls, and in the worst case leave the phone without telephony after every restart. Google has marked the report “Won’t Fix” and treats it as […]

The post Zero-Click ‘SMS of Death’ Flaw Lets Hackers Disrupt Android Phones With a Single Text appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A security researcher has published details of a zero-click Android flaw called “SMS of Death.” One malformed text message can crash the phone service on an Android device, drop active calls, and in the worst case leave the phone without telephony after every restart. Google has marked the report “Won’t Fix” and treats it as a non-security issue, according to the researcher’s disclosure site.

The bug sits in WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu(), the Android code that reads WAP Push messages. These are special data texts that never show up in the inbox. The code reads a header length from the message as a long number and then converts it to a smaller signed integer without checking the range.

The researcher shows that the five bytes 88 80 80 80 00 turn into -2147483648 after this conversion. Android then tries to create a byte array of that size.

That throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException and kills the com.android.phone process. The victim sees nothing. No message appears, and the sender’s number stays hidden.

Zero-Click ‘SMS of Death’ Flaw

Active calls end with the cause CS_DEATH as the process restarts. Each message causes one to two seconds without service. The carrier also resends texts the phone never acknowledges, so one message caused repeated outages for up to a week in testing.

About 20 messages left a phone unusable for a long time. The researcher tested a Pixel 9 on April 2026 firmware, and several Samsung Galaxy and A-series phones, and the crash happened every time.

Android already has other zero-click risks from fake cell towers. Google’s Android 17 adds protections against 2G downgrade and SMS blaster tricks. Those protections target a different problem and do not appear to cover this parsing bug.

Sending about 30 messages in quick succession is far worse. The repeated crashes collide with writes to the SMS store and corrupt the SQLite database that holds messages. After that, the phone app crashes on every boot, and a restart does not help.

A factory reset only works for a short time, because the carrier sends the stuck payload again. The researcher’s fix was to move the physical SIM into a non-Android phone such as an iPhone so the carrier’s retries get acknowledged. Then the corrupt records had to be cleared over ADB. An eSIM would make recovery much harder, and most users could not do it.

Zero-click attacks on phones are not new. In 2023, Citizen Lab found BLASTPASS, an iPhone zero-click chain used to install Pegasus spyware

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?
