The post FBI Seizes Virtualine Bulletproof Hosting Domain Linked to Ransomware and Cybercrime appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The FBI seized virtualine.net, the main website of a bulletproof hosting provider linked to ransomware operators, stolen-data markets, and other cybercrime services.

Announced on October 27, 2026, the court-authorized action targeted a business accused of helping criminals keep their websites online, ignore abuse complaints, and hide payments.

The U.S. Justice Department said Virtualine also operated under the names Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo, and Omegatech. It sold hosting, servers, and domain registration services while openly seeking customers on cybercrime forums.

Investigators linked its services to child sexual abuse material, the sharing of intimate images without consent, and international money laundering.s

Virtualine marketed its willingness to support illegal activity as a selling point. In September 2024, it told an Exploit. user that customers could use its services for phishing, payment card fraud, spam, port scanning, and other illegal activities. Its stated exceptions were child abuse content and terrorism.

By March 2026, the provider was advertising an “additional protection plan” for customers facing law enforcement requests. Under that plan, Virtualine would move a customer’s criminal infrastructure to an unrelated shell company and reactivate the server, according to court records cited by prosecutors.

FBI Seizes Virtualine Bulletproof Hosting

That offer shows how bulletproof hosting can help criminal operations recover from pressure rather than provide server space. Similar concerns appeared in earlier coverage of U.S. sanctions against bulletproof hosting provider Aeza, whose infrastructure supported ransomware and information-stealing malware.

Chainalysis reported that Virtualine’s payment addresses were directly linked to ransomware operators, infostealer infrastructure, Russian-language cybercrime forums, illicit shops, and scam and phishing addresses. These findings provide context for the hosting provider’s role in several types of online crime.

The Justice Department said Virtualine accepted payments through an option labeled “BTC [NO-AML],” using unhosted Bitcoin addresses. Prosecutors allege that Virtualine then laundered payments from criminal customers to hide their source. The announcement did not identify individual ransomware groups or disclose the total value of those transactions.

A central part of the investigation involved a criminal forum identified as Vendor 1. Prosecutors say it sold access to explicit images of minors and adults and promoted hackers who could break into victims’ accounts to steal private material.

Virtualine began receiving warnings about child sexual abuse material in January 2026. Notices came from police in Germany, Canada, and Australia, the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, and a victim’s attorney. Despite those reports, Virtualine allegedly kept the forum online and helped build another site to upload and sell content.

The FBI Washington Field Office led the investigation with German, Dutch, and British authorities, alongside OverRIPE and Lumen. The case follows wider action against criminal hosting, including U.S. charges against two bulletproof hosting companies.

However, taking control of Virtualine’s domain does not establish that every related server stopped operating. Silent Push reported that Omegatech was not fully offline after the seizure.

articles.title: Malicious Firefox Extensions Impersonate Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget to Steal Crypto Wallet Keys
articles.description:
Three malicious Firefox extensions posed as the Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget crypto wallets to steal recovery phrases and private keys. Whoever holds these secrets controls the wallet and every coin in it. All three listings were live on the Firefox Add-ons store during the research and have since been removed. The fake add-ons copied the […]

The post Malicious Firefox Extensions Impersonate Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget to Steal Crypto Wallet Keys appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Three malicious Firefox extensions posed as the Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget crypto wallets to steal recovery phrases and private keys.

Whoever holds these secrets controls the wallet and every coin in it. All three listings were live on the Firefox Add-ons store during the research and have since been removed.

The fake add-ons copied the names, icons, and marketing text of well-known wallets. Anyone searching the store for a trusted wallet could easily install one by mistake. This is the same trick seen in other fake crypto wallet screens used to trap careless users.

Researchers at Socket.dev identified the malware and shared their findings on October 27, 2026. Their team found that the extensions send stolen secrets to subdomains of one command-and-control domain, bonto[.]io.

The Phantom copy also carried a hidden loader that could change its behavior after Mozilla approved it.

Malicious Firefox Extensions Impersonate Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget

The Phantom listing used lookalike Unicode letters in its name, so it appeared on screen as “Phantom.” It reused Phantom’s real ghost icon and called itself “Official Phantom Wallet (Firefox Update).”

The Jupiter copy claimed it was built by Jupiter Exchange. The Bitget copy used the internal name “TabFlow Pro” but showed Bitget branding to users. None of them offered a privacy policy, and all declared that they collect no data.

The Phantom package held a small loader added to its background script. The loader hid its server address inside a list of numbers, then fetched a settings file from phantom[.]bonto[.]io.

That file told the extension whether to run and carried a base64-encoded stealer. The code ran inside every page the victim opened, which let it read the wallet’s own page objects.

Since the operator controls that server, it could return a harmless reply during Mozilla’s review and the real stealer afterward.

The stealer watched for 12, 15, 18, and 24-word recovery phrases, and for Ethereum and Solana private-key formats. It read text boxes, paste events, and the numbered phrase grid that wallets show on their secret-phrase screen.

Captured data was sent to the attacker’s server as JSON. This is not the first time Socket has found this style of theft. It also reported 16 malicious Firefox extensions that copied Rabby and OKX wallet screens earlier this month.

The Jupiter and Bitget fakes worked more simply. They bundled the stealer in the package and sent the recovery phrase straight to jupiter[.]bonto[.]io or bitget[.]bonto[.]io.

The Jupiter copy also asked for access to Trezor Connect, which widened what it could read. Socket noted that all three packages carried a full, always-on stealer inside the signed code Mozilla reviewed, so the remote loader was only an extra layer.

Hidden Infrastructure and Real-World Risk

The Phantom package went further and included the operator’s own drainer backend, a Node.js file named server.js.

It saved stolen secrets to local files, sent them to a Telegram bot, and moved funds to fixed payout addresses on Ethereum, BSC, Polygon, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, Avalanche, Solana, and Bitcoin.

A code comment said the payload would work only “after approval flip,” meaning after Mozilla’s review. A second file, server-review.js, returned an inactive reply while the review was underway.

All the exfiltration servers sit behind Cloudflare, which hides the real host. Socket also found working subdomains for coinbase[.]bonto[.]io and exodus[.]bonto[.]io.

That suggests the group planned to impersonate Coinbase Wallet and Exodus too, although no matching store listings were found. Each fake add-on came from its own throwaway developer account, which makes bulk takedowns slower.

Phantom and Jupiter packages also contained a CLAUDE.md file, an AI jailbreak prompt that was never loaded. Socket says this points to AI-assisted malware writing and an attempt to fool AI-based review.

The campaign also faked its reputation. Over about two days, the Phantom listing’s reviews jumped from 275 to 546, and its rating rose from 2.9 to 3.9.

That pushed down one-star reviews from users who said they lost funds, though those claims are unverified. The listings had only one to three daily users, but the servers were active.

The group looks like a repeat offender, much like the earlier Offside Wallet Theft Factory campaign that Socket tied to 77 Firefox add-ons.

Wallet users should install extensions only through links on the wallet maker’s official website, not through store search. No real wallet will ask for a recovery phrase on a web page.

Anyone who typed a phrase or key into one of these add-ons should create a new wallet on a clean device and move their funds right away.

Deleting the extension does not make a leaked phrase safe. Security teams should block the bonto[.]io domain and its subdomains and look for extensions that fetch settings and then run the result as code.

Browser add-ons are not the only wallet risk. The Odyssey Stealer campaign shows that attackers also hunt wallet data on desktops.

articles.title: Hackers Use Fake Court Notices to Deliver XWorm Malware Through Hidden Windows Scripts
articles.description:
Attackers are sending fake court notices to organizations in Colombia and using them to install XWorm, a remote access tool that gives criminals full control of an infected PC. The emails look like real legal letters. The attached files are hidden Windows scripts that quietly start the infection. The lure works because few people ignore […]

The post Hackers Use Fake Court Notices to Deliver XWorm Malware Through Hidden Windows Scripts appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers are sending fake court notices to organizations in Colombia and using them to install XWorm, a remote access tool that gives criminals full control of an infected PC. The emails look like real legal letters.

The attached files are hidden Windows scripts that quietly start the infection. The lure works because few people ignore a message that says a court case needs urgent attention. The emails are written in Spanish and come from Colombian organizations.

The file names copy real administrative and legal papers, so a busy employee may open the file without a second thought. Behind that file sits a long chain of hidden steps, similar to the new XWorm infection chain seen last year.

Researchers at Arctic Wolf Labs published their findings on GitHub on October 26, 2026. They noted that the campaign targets Colombian organizations.

They also found that the final loader matches one used in a separate September 2026 XWorm case linked to the UK, which suggests the attackers are reusing their tools.

Hackers Use Fake Court Notices

The infection starts with an email that carries a VBScript or JavaScript file. Some files arrive inside ZIP archives, and the second-stage files are downloaded from public file-hosting services such as Filestack and ImageKit.

File names like “ACTA_NOTIFICA_TUTELA.js” and “PROCESO DISCIPLINARIO_ RAD_00470032.vbs” are meant to look like real legal papers.

Courts in Colombia are a common theme for local criminals, and the same trick appeared in Blind Eagle-linked phishing campaigns that also used fake judicial messages.

Once the victim opens the script, it does not show any warning. Instead, it unlocks a hidden PowerShell command. The script is heavily scrambled to avoid detection.

The VBScript version uses a custom Base93 decoder and several layers of encryption, while the JavaScript samples use other encryption methods and randomly generated function names. This makes it very hard for antivirus tools to spot the real purpose of the file.

The hidden PowerShell code then unpacks two files: a .NET DLL called RSG_UnityApp and the XWorm program itself. PowerShell loads the DLL and passes it the path to RegAsm.exe, a trusted Windows tool, along with the XWorm code.

The loader injects XWorm into RegAsm.exe, so the malware runs inside a program that looks normal. Security teams that only watch for unknown files can easily miss this step.

What XWorm Can Do and How to Defend Against It

After it starts, XWorm reads its hidden settings and contacts its command server. It sends back details about the PC, including the user name, system details, hardware, antivirus status, and whether a webcam is present.

Traffic is encrypted with AES-128-ECB, and every message begins with its length followed by a null byte. The researchers saw commands for running shell commands, capturing the screen, managing files, loading plugins, and starting DDoS traffic.

XWorm is sold as a service, so many criminals can buy it, and it often ranks high in weekly malware threat rankings. The researchers found three command servers, and the same servers appear in public sandbox records under different sample hashes and mutexes.

This points to several separate builds that share the same infrastructure. Arctic Wolf also saw the same loader deliver DCRat in another sample.

Defenders should watch for wscript.exe or cscript.exe starting PowerShell, especially with hidden or encoded commands. They should also flag RegAsm.exe when it runs after PowerShell, creates suspended processes, or makes network connections.

Checking DNS and firewall logs for the domains and ports below is a quick way to find infected systems. Staff should confirm any court notice through an official channel and never open unexpected script files, which are among the common XWorm delivery methods.

articles.title: Claude AI Builds One-Click Chrome and 0-Click Linux Exploit Chains, Bypasses Android Lock Screen
articles.description:
Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team says an unreleased Claude research model wrote working exploit chains for Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux. The company shared the details in on research post on October 27, 2026. These were lab tests and not real-world incidents. Anthropic reported every bug to the vendor first, and the vendor released fixes. […]

The post Claude AI Builds One-Click Chrome and 0-Click Linux Exploit Chains, Bypasses Android Lock Screen appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team says an unreleased Claude research model wrote working exploit chains for Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux.

The company shared the details in on research post on October 27, 2026. These were lab tests and not real-world incidents. Anthropic reported every bug to the vendor first, and the vendor released fixes.

Chrome Falls to a One-Click Chain

The Chrome exploit is the most detailed. After a first prompt, Claude wrote a chain that runs code outside the browser sandbox. The test launched the Calculator app on a default Chrome install on macOS within seconds of a page loading.

The chain used four bugs. The first corrupted memory in V8, Chrome’s JavaScript engine. The second broke out of V8’s memory sandbox, beat ASLR, and took over the renderer process. A race condition in CacheStorage then leaked the layout of the more powerful browser process. A use-after-free bug in FedCM, Chrome’s sign-in feature, finished the escape.

Anthropic says Google assigned 62 CVEs, all rated high or critical, including 13 sandbox escapes. All are fixed in Chrome 156. Google’s Chrome 156 release notes from October 20 credit “Xinyang Ge (Anthropic), assisted by Claude” for several fixes, but not for all 62.

Safari and Android Bypasses

In Safari, Claude broke the same-origin policy, the rule that keeps one website from reading another. The chain started with a use-after-free bug in JavaScriptCore. It then got around WebKit’s Gigacage defense and used a flaw in the sandbox’s IPC mechanism to read history, cookies, and sessions from disk. Anthropic notes this chain never needed code execution. A hostile page could read a signed-in email or bank account. Apple confirmed the report the same day and shipped a fix.

The Android case needs physical access. Claude pulled photos and other data from a locked Google Pixel 9 over USB. It did this by linking three flaws that skipped the USB data block, the pairing authorization, and the six-digit code check. A fallback path then sent raw file bytes past a hardcoded block. Anthropic says Google fixed it. Our earlier story on an Android lock screen bypass through Driving Mode shows how often these gaps appear.

Windows Crash Bug and the CVE Mismatch

Claude also found a remote crash bug in Windows, which Anthropic describes as an out-of-bounds read in the kernel’s QUIC code. It reached the bug by reverse engineering a Windows binary with Ghidra. A few packets could crash and restart a server that answers HTTP/3, and repeating them keeps it down. Anthropic believes several million such servers face the internet.

Public records tell a slightly different story. The NVD entry for CVE-2026-33096 names the Windows HTTP.sys driver and not QUIC. It carries a 7.5 score and a fix from April 2026. Rapid7 lists the same details. The NVD entry does not name a finder.

Zero-Click Linux Root Access

The Linux chain is the most serious. Claude wrote an exploit that gives a remote attacker root access on servers running a multipath TCP listener. It needs no login and no user action. It works in two steps. First, it leaks a kernel pointer to defeat KASLR. Then it reuses the same race condition bug to overwrite a callback pointer and run a shell command.

A lost race only fails the handshake and does not crash the machine, so an attacker can try again and again. In the test, the leak took 48 minutes, and the shell took five more. Anthropic ties this to CVE-2026-98432. Its Tenable listing rates it 9.8 and describes an IPv4 TCP use-after-free fix, with no mention of multipath TCP. The link between the two rests on Anthropic’s post.

Anthropic says it found so many bugs by running many scanning agents in parallel and checking each finding with a standard process. It also urges teams to scan code at pull request time, and it released a security guidance plugin for Claude Code. Its expanded Cyber Verification Program gives approved security staff access to its strongest models.

The same tools can help attackers, so patching speed is critical. Update Chrome to version 156 or later, install current Apple, Android, and Windows updates, and patch Linux kernels. Teams can also read our report on Claude Security’s continuous repository scans and our earlier look at chained Claude.ai flaws.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

The post Claude AI Builds One-Click Chrome and 0-Click Linux Exploit Chains, Bypasses Android Lock Screen appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.description:

Attackers are already sending live exploit traffic at Node.js servers, so teams should patch right away. CISA added the bug to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 27, 2026. Federal agencies must fix it by November 10, 2026. CISA […]

The post Node2Shell Vulnerability Actively Exploited in the Wild, CISA Warns appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
CISA has added the Node2Shell flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-111497, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Attackers are already sending live exploit traffic at Node.js servers, so teams should patch right away.

CISA added the bug to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 27, 2026. Federal agencies must fix it by November 10, 2026. CISA lists it as an unchecked return value flaw in Google Brotli. It says a remote attacker with no login can use a crafted Brotli stream to corrupt memory, leak data, crash the app, or possibly run code. CISA marks ransomware use as unknown. It also says forensic triage is not required under BOD 26-04.

The flaw goes by several names. Researchers call it Node2Shell, HTTP2Shell, Broccoli2Shell and Brotli2Shell. Google’s CNA gives it a 9.2 Critical score under CVSS 4.0. The bug is an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder, and Wiz’s technical write-up covers detection and mitigation for cloud teams.

Our own earlier report on the Node2Shell proof of concept covered the first public code execution demo. Things have moved fast since then. Within days, the story went from a lab demo to real attacks.

Node2Shell Vulnerability

Brotli is a compression format that web servers and clients use to shrink traffic. A Brotli stream is split into blocks, and special switch commands tell the decoder which block type comes next. The trouble starts when a kind of block has only one type declared.

A switch in that case is invalid and the decoder should reject it. ELLIO’s research explains that the helper function returned a plain false for this case. It also returned false when the decoder simply ran out of input. Two different problems got the same answer.

When the caller hears that more input is needed, it sends more. The decoder keeps leftover bytes in an internal eight-byte buffer. A real shortage drains that buffer on the next chunk. An invalid switch never drains it. The bytes keep piling up, and past the eighth byte the writes land outside the buffer. Because the write uses a signed 32-bit offset, an attacker can pick a spot within roughly 2 GB and copy 16 bytes of their own data there.

The fix is upstream commit 0ed4268a. It makes the helper return a real error code, BROTLI_DECODER_ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH with value -17, so bad streams stop at once. The bug has been in Brotli since version 1.0.3 in March 2018. ELLIO says the fix sat in the public master branch from February 2026 with no release or advisory for about eight months.

Who Is Affected

Node.js 22.x, 24.x and 26.x are hit, and so are the end-of-life 20.x, 23.x and 25.x lines. The old lines will get no fix. Fixed Node.js versions are 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. Google fixed Brotli in 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1.

A bare Node.js server does not unpack a Brotli body just because it arrives. Something has to pass the bytes to the decoder. ELLIO describes three common paths. The first is an inbound request with Content-Encoding set to br. Express 5 with express.json() or express.raw(), body-parser 2 and Koa with @koa/bodyparser all unpack it before any route code runs.

The second is an outbound fetch. Built-in fetch(), axios, got, and SuperAgent will decode a hostile server’s reply, so link previews, webhooks, and crawlers are all at risk. The third is any direct node:zlib call on client data.

The problem reaches well past Node.js. Bun before 1.4.4 is affected, and so are the Python packages Brotli and brotlicffi, which need 1.2.1 and 1.2.1.0. Envoy, the Ruby brotli gem, and many Linux distributions are also on the list. The CIS advisory says the flaw sits in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms. Tenable’s FAQ lists affected products in one place.

One trap is worth knowing. Node.js cherry-picked the fix without changing the bundled version string. So process.versions.brotli shows 1.2.0 on both patched and unpatched builds. Check the Node.js release number instead.

Imperva’s Red Team showed the first working exploit on October 22. They ran code on the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image, using both fetch() and Express 5 request bodies. Their write-up, Node2Shell: From Brotli Data to Remote Code Execution, says version 24.22.1 rejected the same input.

ELLIO then repeated the attack on x86-64. It got a shell on four targets running the same build. These were a plain node:http server, the official node:24.22.0-slim image running as root, Express 5.3.0, and Koa 3. Each shell ran as the service’s own account.

The lab found that official Node.js builds are non-PIE, so the binary loads at the same address every time. Address space layout randomization still shuffles the heap and stacks, so an attacker has to guess. With ASLR on, a shell appeared at around attempt 5. With ASLR off, 60 attempts gave no hit. Turning it off does not help.

Two target-specific values decide success. One is the number of the accepted socket, which the shell uses for input and output. The other is a memory offset tied to one exact Node.js build. The offset for 24.22.0 gave nothing against 22.23.3 or 26.12.0 in 10,000 tries. That limits attackers to waves aimed at one popular build at a time.

Scanning began first. A checker calling itself node2shell-check/1.0 hit ELLIO’s sensors from AS44620. It sent 20 Brotli bodies in two bursts to find hosts that decompress Brotli at all. None carried the real trigger. This looked like list building ahead of an attack.

Exploit traffic followed on October 26 at 15:08 UTC. ELLIO saw a single 23,069,983-byte request with SHA-256 7fcbdaaecd4419e2930927844f3b772668204737a4e7602a2290c991c93c5c4b. It came from 94.154.43.7, an address ELLIO rates as malicious with high confidence.

The address was first seen in December 2025 and was active on 47 of the last 90 days. It has been tied to PHP2Shell exploitation, Palo Alto GlobalProtect and FortiOS SSL VPN probing, and Kubernetes scanning. The request targets only Node.js v24.22.0 on x86-64.

The delivery layer copies public exploit code. The ROP chain, which takes over the process, is original. It plants /bin/sh in its own data and calls Node’s execvp from there. It does not use the string already inside Node, as both public chains do.

ELLIO tested it against a clean vulnerable target and got zero shells in 50 attempts. The chain crashed the process instead. ELLIO thinks this was a first try fired before the operator tested the last step. It warns that the operator looks focused on mass exploitation. Teams that remember React2Shell will see the same pattern of fast public code followed by quick scanning. Microsoft documented that earlier flaw in its React2Shell defense guide.

Failed attempts are not harmless. ELLIO saw that most of its 400 Express attempts crashed the worker instead of giving a shell. A crash can write a core dump, and that dump may hold session cookies, tokens and keys from other visitors.

On a stock Ubuntu host, systemd-coredump saves these files in /var/lib/systemd/coredump. Containers usually write nothing, so the harm there is only downtime. Some other decoders hang quietly instead. Python Brotli 1.2.0, brotlicffi 1.2.0.0, the PHP streaming API and the Ruby gem all return nothing and never finish, and the PHP case spins at 100% CPU.

Patch first. Move Node.js to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1, and update Bun, Python packages, Envoy, and any distro Brotli library. Debian users should look for DLA-4855-1 or DSA-6582-1. Alpine users need brotli 1.2.1-r0, or 1.1.1-r0 on 3.21. Leave the old 20.x, 23.x and 25.x lines behind, since they will never be fixed.

A Node.js upgrade only fixes the copied Node bundles. Tools with their own copy, like bun build –compile executables, DuckDB, and PHP extensions, need separate updates. Rebuild images, refresh lockfiles, and restart processes.

A Dockerfile that pins 24.22.0 keeps shipping the bad build until someone edits that line. Check staging, CI, serverless, and developer laptops too.

Until patching is done, block inbound Content-Encoding: br where you can. Also watch logs for large Brotli POST bodies, repeated worker crashes, and the IP and hash above. Limit who can read core dumps, and shorten how long you keep them. Federal teams face the November 10 deadline, but every other team should treat that date as a ceiling and not a goal.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

The post Node2Shell Vulnerability Actively Exploited in the Wild, CISA Warns appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: Veeam Patches Critical Backup & Replication Authorization Bypass Vulnerability
articles.description:
Veeam released security fixes for a critical authorization bypass vulnerability in Veeam Backup & Replication that lets an attacker without login credentials bypass access checks on the CDP Coordinator Service. Tracked as CVE-2026-108142, the flaw carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.1 and affects both Windows-based deployments and the Veeam Software Appliance. The company disclosed […]

The post Veeam Patches Critical Backup & Replication Authorization Bypass Vulnerability appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Veeam released security fixes for a critical authorization bypass vulnerability in Veeam Backup & Replication that lets an attacker without login credentials bypass access checks on the CDP Coordinator Service.

Tracked as CVE-2026-108142, the flaw carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.1 and affects both Windows-based deployments and the Veeam Software Appliance.

The company disclosed the issue on October 27, 2026, in its security advisory KB4948. The advisory also covers two medium-severity file-write vulnerabilities in Backup & Replication and a high-severity local privilege escalation flaw in Veeam Agent for Linux. HackerOne reported all four issues.

CVE-2026-108142 affects Veeam Backup & Replication 13.1.1.18 and earlier builds in the 13.1 branch, along with 13.0.2.29 and earlier builds in the 13.0 branch. Veeam identifies version 12.x as unaffected by this issue.

The flaw concerns authorization, the checks that decide which actions a caller can perform. Veeam says an unauthenticated attacker can bypass those checks on the CDP Coordinator Service.

However, the advisory does not describe the attack sequence or state that the vulnerability enables remote code execution. It also does not report active exploitation.

Veeam Patches Backup & Replication Vulnerability

Veeam lists the first fixed releases as Backup & Replication 13.1.2, build 13.1.2.57, and Backup & Replication 13.0.3, build 13.0.3.63. Administrators should match their installed version against these build numbers rather than checking only the main product version.

The update also addresses CVE-2026-108140 and CVE-2026-108141, each rated medium severity with a CVSS v4.0 score of 5.9. Both require an authenticated user with the Restore Operator role who also controls the contents of a backed-up network-attached storage (NAS) share.

Under those conditions, an attacker can use relative path traversal to write attacker-controlled files to an arbitrary path on the backup server. In simple terms, the file path can escape its intended folder. Veeam lists the same affected Backup & Replication builds and fixed releases for both vulnerabilities.

The separate Linux issue, CVE-2026-105477, has a high-severity score of 7.3. It allows local privilege escalation and affects only Veeam Agent for Linux installations managed by Backup & Replication. Affected releases include 13.1.1.4 and earlier 13.1 builds. The fix starts with version 13.1.2, build 13.1.2.11.

Cyber Security News previously reported attackers exploiting CVE-2024-40711 in Veeam to deploy Frag ransomware, highlighting backup security risks, though this separate vulnerability does not confirm exploitation of the newly disclosed authorization bypass.

The publication also reported Veeam’s October security update for version 12.3.2, noting that different product branches may require different patches.

Administrators can check their installed Backup & Replication build through Help > About in the console. Veeam’s release information page provides update guidance.

The company warns that attackers may study released patches to find ways into unpatched systems, making timely installation important across affected backup servers and managed Linux agents.

The incidents followed a similar pattern: attackers gained access through the camera application, […]

The post Hackers Compromise Camera Management Software to Deploy Malware on Windows Computers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers have compromised camera management software to deploy malware on Windows computers, using a legitimate Microsoft program to run malicious code and maintain access.

The activity shows how software used to manage surveillance systems can become an entry point into business networks. The incidents followed a similar pattern: attackers gained access through the camera application, deployed a suspected reverse shell, and used DLL sideloading to contact an outside server.

Like earlier cases involving abuse of monitoring tools, the activity highlights risks surrounding software trusted for routine operations.

Researchers from Huntress identified the malware activity across several customer environments during September and October 2026.

In their October 27 investigation, Harlan Carvey and Lindsey O’Donnell-Welch described a handful of incidents linked to compromised camera management software, while noting important gaps in understanding the initial break-in.

Hackers Compromise Camera Management Software

The affected application lacked embedded file version information, preventing researchers from confirming its full product name or developer.

They also could not locate application logs, leaving the exact method used to compromise the software unresolved. The report does not identify a specific vulnerability or CVE.

Investigators found strings connecting the executable to a domain associated with Korean company 3R Global. A camera management package available through another website contained matching strings.

However, Huntress stressed that these overlaps did not establish the vendor’s identity or prove where affected customers obtained their software.

After gaining access, attackers placed an executable inside a user’s application data directory. Its command line specified a remote address, a connection port, and authentication values.

Combined with its location in a writable folder, these details led researchers to assess the program as a reverse shell. The attackers then copied Windows Parental Control Monitor into another application data folder.

Huntress verified that this executable was a genuine Microsoft file, but its unusual location exposed the abuse. Similar VLC and VMware sideloading cases demonstrate why a trusted executable alone cannot establish that nearby libraries are safe.

Here, the Microsoft program loaded malicious DLLs placed alongside it. The libraries resembled legitimate zlib compression components but had been modified to periodically contact a command-and-control server.

This technique, called DLL sideloading, lets attackers execute their code through an otherwise legitimate application.

The distinction matters because the executable itself was not the malicious payload. Its role was to load attacker-controlled libraries from the surrounding folder.

Checking the Microsoft file’s identity without examining its location, loaded DLLs, parent process, and network activity would leave out the evidence that connected an apparently normal Windows component to the wider infection chain.

Persistence, Detection, and Defensive Priorities

Attackers maintained access by adding the relocated Microsoft executable to the user’s Run registry key. Windows would then launch it whenever that user signed in, restarting the loading chain.

Every investigated incident involved communication with the same command-and-control IP address listed below. For defenders, the most useful signal is the connected sequence of events rather than any single filename.

Camera software launching an unexpected executable, followed by a Microsoft component running from a writable folder and making unusual outbound connections, warrants investigation. Huntress specifically recommends examining that process chain.

Organizations should inventory camera management applications, restrict access, and monitor their network activity. Earlier EggStreme DLL sideloading attacks also abused a Windows executable from an application data folder, reinforcing the value of checking execution locations.

Where practical, Huntress recommends application controls that block unapproved executables and DLLs in user-writable directories. The investigation also leaves limits on what organizations can conclude.

Huntress did not establish how the initial camera software compromise occurred, and the available evidence does not justify describing this as a confirmed vendor supply-chain breach.

The immediate lesson is narrower: camera management applications need the same endpoint oversight as other business software, rather than being overlooked entirely.

articles.description:
Hackers have begun testing a critical Oracle E-Business Suite vulnerability that can let them run commands without logging in. Threat intelligence firm Defused reported exploratory exploit attempts against its decoy systems on October 27, 2026. However, these observations do not confirm successful attacks against customer systems, and Oracle had already released a patch before the […]

The post Hackers Actively Exploiting New Oracle EBS RCE Vulnerability appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers have begun testing a critical Oracle E-Business Suite vulnerability that can let them run commands without logging in. Threat intelligence firm Defused reported exploratory exploit attempts against its decoy systems on October 27, 2026.

However, these observations do not confirm successful attacks against customer systems, and Oracle had already released a patch before the activity was detected.

Tracked as CVE-2026-101767, the flaw carries a critical CVSS score of 9.8. Horizon3.ai discovered the issue and reported it to Oracle on July 24. Oracle fixed it on October 20 through its October Critical Patch Update. Although initially reported privately as a zero-day, it was a publicly disclosed, patched vulnerability when Defused observed the probes.

Oracle EBS 0-Day Vulnerability

The weakness affects the Core component of Oracle Application Object Library in EBS versions 12.2.3 through 12.2.15. It requires network access over HTTP or HTTPS but needs neither valid credentials nor user interaction. Cyber Security News previously covered the issue in its report on Oracle’s October security update.

According to Horizon3.ai’s technical advisory, the vulnerable Thin Client Framework servlet is reachable at /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer. A crafted request can trigger SQL injection, allowing an attacker to send database commands as the powerful APPS database user. That access can then be chained into operating system command execution under the EBS application account.

The impact extends beyond database access. Successful exploitation could expose or alter financial, payroll, human resources, and purchasing records accessible to APPS. Commands run with the application account’s permissions, rather than automatically granting full administrative control over the host.

Defused described the October 27 traffic as “exploratory exploits” against its Oracle EBS decoys. According to reports, no other public reports of exploitation had surfaced. This supports reporting active exploit attempts, but not confirmed breaches, stolen data, or a widespread campaign.

The distinction matters because Oracle EBS has faced damaging attacks before. Cyber Security News documented Cl0p exploitation of a separate Oracle EBS zero-day, CVE-2025-61882. That earlier campaign should not be confused with the newly observed TCF servlet probes.

Administrators should apply the relevant October patches promptly. Until then, Horizon3.ai recommends removing the servlet from the EBS URL firewall allowlist and restricting web access to trusted networks. The default URL firewall permits the endpoint, making configuration checks important.

Defenders should review unauthenticated POST requests invoking GanttDataServer, especially when followed by database queries. Other warning signs include unexpected files in $APPLPTMP and the oracle account launching /bin/sh through Concurrent Manager. Access restrictions reduce exposure but do not replace patching.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

The researchers examined 1,703 configuration-report files containing 101,419 credential and account records associated with 1,689 host identifiers. The material also […]

The post FortiBleed 2.0 Reveals Thousands of Fortinet VPN and Active Directory Credentials in Exposed Configurations appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
FortiBleed 2.0 investigation, published October 27, revealed 40,573 cleartext secret records in exposed FortiGate configurations, including 37,076 local-user passwords and 1,576 Active Directory LDAP bind records linking firewall access, VPN services, and internal identity systems.

The researchers examined 1,703 configuration-report files containing 101,419 credential and account records associated with 1,689 host identifiers.

The material also includes administrator logins, email-server passwords, and high-availability cluster secrets. These figures reflect records, not unique users, confirmed physical devices, or credentials that still work today.

Despite its name, FortiBleed 2.0 is a follow-up investigation based on recently obtained files, not a newly disclosed vulnerability. Most files are dated February 20, 2026, while 31 are undated, leaving the timing of initial access and configuration theft unconfirmed.

FortiBleed 2.0 Exposes Fortinet VPN and AD Credentials

Compared with the first dataset, researchers identified 924 additional host identifiers and 975 domain labels absent from the earlier collection.

However, domain labels can belong to service providers, registration contacts, or account holders. They should not be read as 975 newly compromised companies. The findings expand earlier FortiBleed credential exposure coverage by revealing accounts and services behind perimeter logins.

The associated toolchain extracts firewall configurations, recovers stored secrets, and attempts further access. Its parsing workflow collects local users, administrator entries, LDAP connections, cluster settings, and email credentials.

Some stored FortiOS ENC values can be recovered offline when configurations use the system-default encryption key. Recovery depends on the software version, settings, and available material.

Exposed local-user passwords may support VPN access, but account status, access rules, reachability, and multifactor authentication determine whether login succeeds.

Hudson Rock’s analysis identified 7,437 disabled local-user records containing cleartext data. Empty MFA fields do not necessarily indicate missing MFA, as external authentication systems may enforce it.

LDAP bind credentials deserve close attention because they connect FortiGate appliances to directory services. An account with excessive rights could increase the impact of a breach.

Ordinary LDAP query access, however, does not automatically grant domain-administrator privileges. Earlier reporting on FortiGate configuration theft highlights this route toward internal access.

Fortinet’s response guidance calls for terminating administrator and VPN sessions, resetting credentials, enforcing MFA, updating firmware, and restricting management access.

Security teams should compare current settings with a trusted configuration and examine firewall and domain-controller logs for unexpected activity. The configuration findings also call for reviewing LDAP bind passwords, cluster secrets, and email-server credentials.

Investigators should verify ownership of recurring administrator accounts such as fgtsecure and forticloud-sync before treating them as unauthorized. Account names alone do not establish malicious activity.

articles.description:
Microsoft released emergency Windows trust updates after discovering eight recoverable eMudhra intermediate CA private keys that could let attackers forge trusted certificates or sign malicious content. Microsoft said the issue affected eMudhra’s certificate hierarchy, not Microsoft systems. The response includes an October 26 out-of-band Windows update removing seven certificates from the Windows trust list. Microsoft […]

The post Microsoft Releases Emergency Windows Updates to Block Compromised eMudhra Certificates appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft released emergency Windows trust updates after discovering eight recoverable eMudhra intermediate CA private keys that could let attackers forge trusted certificates or sign malicious content.

Microsoft said the issue affected eMudhra’s certificate hierarchy, not Microsoft systems. The response includes an October 26 out-of-band Windows update removing seven certificates from the Windows trust list.

Microsoft confirmed on October 27 that it had removed the same certificates from the Microsoft Edge trust list, extending its response beyond earlier blocks against the compromised intermediates.

Six affected keys relate to Transport Layer Security, or TLS, which helps protect connections to websites and services. The other two relate to code signing, which helps systems check who published software. Recovering these keys could let attackers misuse the trust attached to their certificate authorities.

An attacker using a compromised TLS key could create a certificate to impersonate a website or service and potentially intercept communications. The code-signing keys could make malicious software appear to come from a trusted publisher. These are potential uses of the keys, not proof that such attacks occurred.

Microsoft Updates to Block eMudhra Certificates

Cyber Security News previously covered the eMudhra certificate authority compromise and the blocks introduced across major platforms. Its reporting on abuse of Microsoft Artifact Signing also shows why a trusted software signature does not guarantee that a file is safe.

Microsoft first updated the Windows Disallowed Certificate Trust List on October 20 to block the affected certificate authorities. It also deployed a separate CRLSet update for Edge and WebView2 to block affected TLS certificates. That browser protection arrives automatically through component updates without requiring a new browser version.

The later Windows update removes six eMudhra G3 root certificates and an AAA Certificate Services cross-sign. Removing these seven certificates is a broader trust decision, separate from blocking the eight compromised intermediate keys and from eMudhra’s revocation of the affected intermediate certificates.

Microsoft warned against restoring trust locally without assessing the risks. Software that does not reliably check certificate revocation or Microsoft’s disallowed list could still accept certificates linked to the compromised intermediates if the removed trust is retained or restored.

Organizations should allow Windows certificate trust updates and Edge component updates to reach managed devices. Disconnected Windows systems need special attention because administrators must provide an alternative way to update.

Microsoft’s certificate trust guidance explains how to distribute trusted and disallowed certificate lists through internal infrastructure.

Microsoft also urged customers to review disconnected Azure virtual machines and Virtual Machine Scale Sets. Updated images are available through Azure Marketplace.

Certificate owners should identify chains that depend on the seven removed certificates and obtain replacements or an alternative trusted chain.

Microsoft is evaluating remaining eMudhra roots separately as customers move away from affected hierarchies. Administrators can monitor Microsoft Trusted Root Program announcements for published changes and verify that certificate updates reach every managed system.

articles.description:
Hackers have abused CyberStrikeAI, an open-source penetration-testing platform, to coordinate 44 AI agents across network scanning, exploitation, persistence, and data theft. The activity primarily targeted Japanese organizations, showing how attackers can turn security tools into repeatable intrusion workflows without developing new vulnerabilities or manually directing every task. During a short period in October 2026, the […]

The post Hackers Use CyberStrikeAI Agents to Automate Network Scanning, Exploitation, and Data Theft appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers have abused CyberStrikeAI, an open-source penetration-testing platform, to coordinate 44 AI agents across network scanning, exploitation, persistence, and data theft.

The activity primarily targeted Japanese organizations, showing how attackers can turn security tools into repeatable intrusion workflows without developing new vulnerabilities or manually directing every task.

During a short period in October 2026, the platform checked weaknesses at at least 19 organizations, including 16 in Japan.

Earlier reporting on CyberStrikeAI attacks against FortiGate devices documented separate abuse of the same tool, although shared software does not establish a connection between the operators behind these campaigns.

Researchers from TrendAI, Bakuei Matsukawa and Joseph C Chen, identified the malicious activity while examining publicly accessible files on attacker-controlled servers.

Their October 27 research report distinguishes CyberStrikeAI’s autonomous workflow from two other operations using AI for planning or scripting. The platform is a legitimate testing tool, not a newly discovered malware family.

Hackers Use CyberStrikeAI Agents

The exposed CyberStrikeAI environment connected reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery, validation, exploitation, command and control, persistence, exfiltration, and reporting.

Instead of leaving an operator to move results between tools, the framework assigned work to specialized agents and recorded their findings in a database, creating a repeatable process across multiple targets.

One recovered entry, “credential-search agent 8/44,” confirmed a configuration involving 44 agents. Different agents searched for credentials, investigated vulnerabilities, attempted exploitation, and handled exfiltration.

The platform generated structured reports and produced Japanese-language forms and fake login pages, helping operators adapt their material to the organizations they targeted.

Its management dashboard displayed tool execution success rates, token usage, and batch creation controls. Each identifiable target had a consistently formatted report and an evidence index.

These records supported TrendAI’s assessment that AI drove the workflow, rather than merely helping a human operator write occasional commands or summarize results.

The same coordination model has legitimate uses: platforms such as ThreatBook’s multi-agent testing platform bring automated agents together for authorized assessments.

In the malicious CyberStrikeAI deployment, however, agents worked across organizations in parallel while limiting traffic sent to each target. That distribution made activity harder to recognize from one organization’s logs alone.

The strongest intrusion evidence began with an unauthenticated administration interface exposed on a legacy web system. No novel vulnerability was involved.

Crucially, validation activity did not mean every organization was breached: many reports explicitly recorded “no session, no web shell, no exfiltration,” and deep compromise affected only a small proportion.

What the Evidence Means for Detection and Defense

TrendAI reconstructed the activity from open directories containing scripts, target lists, logs, command histories, and attack results.

Researchers did not have victim-side logs, disk images, or network records. The findings therefore establish what attackers prepared, attempted, and recorded, but cannot independently confirm every claimed success or the full damage.

The other cases illustrate why AI involvement needs careful labeling. In one human-led operation, an LLM helped develop tools and attack plans, while the operator retained control.

Confirmed theft of property records, commercial information, Windows credentials, and email belonged to that separate case, not the CyberStrikeAI operation.

Another infrastructure showed high-confidence signs of AI-assisted scripting, but researchers lacked direct prompts or API keys confirming its use.

Comparable reporting on AI-generated Linux credential theft scripts also separates suspected code-generation assistance from autonomous execution. Neatly organized comments or emoji may support an assessment, but they do not establish that AI controlled an entire intrusion.

For defenders, the practical priorities remain familiar: inventory public-facing applications, patch or isolate legacy systems, remove unnecessary administration interfaces, and replace default credentials.

Monitoring should account for low-frequency, distributed attempts. TrendAI also recommends reviewing VPN configurations and exposed AI services, reflecting weaknesses observed across its three investigations.

The attackers’ identities, underlying AI models, and any relationship between the three infrastructures remain unresolved.

Simplified Chinese was the working language across the environments, but TrendAI cautioned that language alone cannot establish location or affiliation. Its central finding concerns scale and coordination, not proof of a new state-backed campaign.

articles.description:
Coinbase has disclosed that a security incident at analytics provider Amplitude exposed contact information belonging to a small subset of its customers. The cryptocurrency exchange said it found no evidence of unauthorized access to Coinbase systems and confirmed that customer funds were not impacted. In its official statement, Coinbase Support said the incident also affected […]

The post Coinbase Customer Data Exposed Via Analytics Vendor Amplitude Security Incident appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Coinbase has disclosed that a security incident at analytics provider Amplitude exposed contact information belonging to a small subset of its customers. The cryptocurrency exchange said it found no evidence of unauthorized access to Coinbase systems and confirmed that customer funds were not impacted.

In its official statement, Coinbase Support said the incident also affected other Amplitude customers. The company is notifying impacted users and regulatory agencies under its legal obligations. However, its public update did not identify the other businesses involved or explain how the exposure happened.

“Coinbase has not had a data breach,” the company said, drawing a distinction between its own systems and information held by an outside provider. That distinction matters because customer data can be exposed through a vendor without attackers gaining access to the exchange itself.

Coinbase Customer Data Exposed

Coinbase has not confirmed the number of affected customers or provided a complete list of exposed data fields. Reports have mentioned email addresses and phone numbers, but the official statement refers only to customer contact data. Readers should not treat those reported fields as a confirmed inventory.

Reporting by Cryptopolitan cited a claim from SlowMist security researcher 23pds that more than 70,000 users were affected. Coinbase has not verified that figure. Its statement also did not name an attacker, disclose an entry method, or establish when the Amplitude incident began.

Coinbase’s statement does not say that passwords, private keys, or transaction records were exposed. It also does not provide a detailed technical account of the incident. Those gaps make it important to separate confirmed company statements from broader claims circulating online about the event.

The Coinbase Amplitude security incident highlights third-party risk. Analytics services help businesses understand how people use their products. When customer information reaches an outside provider, the security of that provider becomes part of the wider data protection picture, even when the main platform remains secure.

This event should not be confused with the separate Coinbase data theft disclosed in May 2025. Cyber Security News reported that attackers paid overseas support personnel to obtain customer information in that earlier case. There is no established connection between that incident and the current Amplitude exposure.

Contact data alone does not provide direct access to cryptocurrency wallets. However, it can help scammers reach customers with convincing messages about account restrictions, suspicious transactions, or urgent security checks. Knowing that someone uses Coinbase can make a fake support message seem more believable and harder to dismiss.

Cyber Security News previously covered another Coinbase cyberattack involving employees targeted with fake messages. That earlier case provides context for the risks of impersonation, but it does not establish how the Amplitude incident occurred. No public evidence reviewed for this report confirms phishing caused this vendor incident.

Customers should check security notices through the Coinbase app or by visiting its website directly rather than following unexpected links. Coinbase’s support scam guidance says staff will never ask for passwords or verification codes, request remote access, or tell customers to send cryptocurrency to an external address.

The immediate concern is therefore possible follow-up fraud, not a confirmed compromise of Coinbase wallets. Affected users should review their notification for specific details and remain cautious about unsolicited contact. Further disclosures are needed to establish the full scope of the exposure, the information involved, and the cause of the incident.

The post CISA Warns of PHP2Shell Vulnerabilities Actively Exploited in Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has added two critical PHP vulnerabilities, jointly known as PHP2Shell, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after confirming real-world exploitation.

The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, can let unauthenticated attackers remotely execute code on vulnerable PHP web servers.

CISA added both issues to the KEV catalog on October 26 and urged organizations to treat them as an urgent patching priority. The agency said the vulnerabilities pose significant risk because attackers can target web-facing systems without needing valid login credentials.

Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies must complete mitigation or take affected products out of service by October 29 under Binding Operational Directive 26-04.

CVE-2026-109618 is described as a PHP memory corruption issue. It occurs when PHP encounters an out-of-memory condition and leaves some internal request data in an unsafe state.

CVE-2026-109619 is a stale internal request-state issue where PHP can retain references to memory that has already been released. Under certain conditions, an attacker can use either weakness to gain remote code execution on an exposed server.

PHP2Shell Vulnerabilities Actively Exploited

The flaws affect PHP deployments used to serve web applications, including systems running PHP through common web server setups.

Security researchers warn that both issues may be especially serious in environments where PHP workers process repeated requests, since attackers may trigger the vulnerable state and then send follow-up requests to gain code execution.

Successful exploitation could allow a threat actor to run commands with the permissions assigned to the PHP web worker. PHP released fixes in versions 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12. Organizations running older supported branches should upgrade to the matching fixed release immediately.

Teams using PHP 5.x, 7.x, or 8.0 and 8.1 should review their hosting platform or operating system vendor guidance because the PHP project no longer maintains those branches.

CISA’s warning matters because inclusion in the KEV catalog means evidence shows attackers are already exploiting the bugs. Security teams should not treat PHP2Shell as a routine software update.

Internet-facing PHP servers should be identified first, then patched and restarted so the updated runtime is loaded. Administrators should also check application logs, web server logs, PHP-FPM logs, process activity, and outbound network connections for unusual behavior that may indicate compromise before the update was applied.

Web application firewalls may reduce some malicious requests, but they don’t replace updating PHP. Organizations should also review third-party products, hosting panels, container images, and cloud workloads that package their own PHP runtime. Vendor-supplied software may need a separate update even when the base operating system has been patched.

Readers can also follow Cyber Security News coverage of CISA security developments and monitor the CISA KEV Catalog for newly exploited flaws. For technical details and patch guidance, administrators should review CISA’s PHP2Shell alert.

articles.description:
Hackers have abused government and school domains to promote illegal gambling websites, creating unauthorized subdomains while leaving the institutions’ main websites running normally. Two unrelated operations used changes to Domain Name System (DNS) records to place gambling pages beneath trusted institutional addresses, borrowing their reputation to attract visitors through search results. The activity affected institutions […]

The post Hackers Hijack Government and School Subdomains to Promote Illegal Gambling Websites appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers have abused government and school domains to promote illegal gambling websites, creating unauthorized subdomains while leaving the institutions’ main websites running normally.

Two unrelated operations used changes to Domain Name System (DNS) records to place gambling pages beneath trusted institutional addresses, borrowing their reputation to attract visitors through search results.

The activity affected institutions in Bangladesh, India, and Mexico. One operation involved more than 850 observed entry points across eight institutional domains and connections to over 30 gambling brands.

These figures describe infrastructure, not confirmed victims or infections, and researchers consider them minimum counts because their investigation was continuing.

Researchers from Infoblox identified the two operations and detailed their findings in an October 26, 2026, report on domain shadowing.

The research describes DNS abuse supporting illegal gambling promotion, rather than a newly identified malware family. How the attackers initially gained access to DNS administration remains unknown.

Hackers Hijack Government and School Subdomains

Domain shadowing allows attackers to add unauthorized DNS records beneath a legitimate domain without changing its main website.

Unlike the previously reported Hazy Hawk subdomain hijacking activity involving abandoned cloud resources, these operations appear to involve unauthorized access to DNS administration. That distinction matters when investigating how control was obtained.

Infoblox tracks the first actor as Hidden Hawk, which appears to sell search visibility to illegal Indonesian gambling brands.

The actor added CNAME records, which make one hostname an alias for another, beneath school and government domains. Most pointed to gambling content hosted externally on Cloudflare Pages rather than institutional servers.

The external hosting names often copied the corresponding institutional hostname, replacing dots with hyphens. This pattern helped researchers reconstruct relationships between the hijacked addresses and hosted pages.

In one documented example, gambling content remained accessible beneath a Bangladeshi secondary school’s domain between July 6 and October 1, 2026.

The use of legitimate hosting services also appears in separate Cloudflare Pages scam campaigns that exploit readily available infrastructure. Here, the important feature was the connection between externally hosted gambling pages and trusted institutional addresses.

Website checks alone could miss the activity because the schools’ and government offices’ primary services remained available. Six Bangladeshi school domains carried approximately 50 to more than 240 entries each, while a Mexican educational domain had over 50.

A Kerala government subdomain hosted gambling content directly and received some school CNAME connections. Researchers observed the Kerala case as remediated in July 2026, although some other infrastructure remained active.

During controlled research, Infoblox contacted a Telegram account believed to belong to Hidden Hawk using a fabricated casino identity.

The operator offered backlink optimization, custom landing pages, and Google AMP pages, supplied payment details, and guaranteed a top Google ranking. Researchers made no payment; the sales pitch matched the infrastructure they observed.

Government DNS Delegations Expanded Attacker Control

The second operation targeted Maharashtra government infrastructure and an ESIC subdomain in India. Rather than adding individual aliases, the attackers created unauthorized nameserver delegations to ClouDNS.

This transferred authority over selected DNS subzones to external nameservers, allowing records beneath them to be managed outside the government’s normal DNS environment. Infoblox has not attributed this activity to Hidden Hawk.

A wildcard record expanded that control by allowing arbitrary names beneath one delegated subzone to resolve.

Gambling-related records appeared from at least August 2025. Content delivery involved DigitalOcean, Amazon CloudFront, and BunnyCDN, with machine-generated doorway pages covering rummy, betting, lotteries, and satta matka.

The delegations disappeared by mid-October 2026, suggesting remediation. The findings add to concerns about gambling infrastructure, although separate casino sites concealing espionage demonstrate a different use of similar-looking content.

In this investigation, the documented purpose was search visibility and traffic acquisition. The evidence does not establish that visitors received malware, or that either operation stole institutional data.

For defenders, the priority is monitoring authoritative DNS changes, not simply checking whether a homepage looks normal.

Unexpected CNAME targets, new nameserver delegations, unexplained wildcard records, and bursts of unfamiliar subdomains require investigation. Certificate-transparency observations should also be compared with approved services and DNS change records.

Organizations discovering unauthorized changes should remove the offending records, review registrar and DNS-provider logs, rotate exposed credentials, and enforce multifactor authentication.

Infoblox cautions against blocking entire legitimate institutional domains. Response should focus on unauthorized hostnames and attacker-controlled infrastructure while addressing the account access or delegation that enabled the abuse. Shared hosting platforms likewise require contextual investigation rather than blanket blocking.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Prevention lost; now what? That question not backup-window math defines ransomware recovery, a discipline measured in hours-to-business and judged on three hard problems: finding the clean restore point, proving it’s actually clean, and rebuilding at scale without reinfecting yourself.

We scored ten platforms specifically on the recovery day, not the backup night. Rubrik takes 1; Veeam and HPE Zerto complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Rubrik clean-point identification and blast-radius analytics built for the worst day.

• Podium: Rubrik (recovery intelligence), Veeam (verified restores at breadth), Zerto (near-zero RPO rewind).

• Different metric than backup: this list ranks hours-to-business after an attack, not protection breadth see our Backup & Recovery ranking for that lens.

• Reinfection is the silent second incident: clean-room staging and snapshot scanning separate real recovery platforms from restore buttons.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation: clean-point identification (anomaly/encryption analytics on snapshots), restore verification and clean-room staging, recovery speed at scale (mass-restore orchestration, failover), blast-radius and sensitive-data assessment, and pricing structure.

No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Weights: clean-point intelligence 30%, recovery speed 25%, verification/clean-room 20%, orchestration maturity 15%, pricing clarity 10%.

The 2026 Ransomware Recovery Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Rubrik — Best Recovery Intelligence

Snapshot: Subscription | Anomaly detection, blast-radius, sensitive-data exposure | Default-immutable

Why it earns 1: Recovery day is an intelligence problem before it’s a restore problem, and Rubrik answers the three questions that matter fastest: when did encryption start (anomaly timeline), what did the attacker touch (blast radius), and what data was exposed (sensitive-data discovery on snapshots).

clean-point selection backed by that evidence turns a guessing game into a procedure.

Pros: Best-in-class clean-point analytics; immutability by default; quarantine-aware restores.

Cons: Premium pricing; full value on its platform model.

Bottom line: The worst-day decision-support leader.

2. Veeam — Best Verified Restore at Breadth

Snapshot: Subscription | SureBackup verification, malware scanning, orchestrated DR | Broadest estate reach

Why it earns 2: Veeam proves restores before the crisis automated recovery verification, malware scanning on backup data, and orchestrated recovery plans across more workload types than anyone.

When the estate is heterogeneous, Veeam is usually the platform that can actually rebuild all of it.

Pros: Verification discipline; orchestration (Recovery Orchestrator); estate breadth.

Cons: Deepest analytics arrived later than Rubrik’s.

Bottom line: Rehearsed recovery across everything you run.

3. HPE (Zerto) — Best Near-Zero RPO Rewind

Snapshot: Quote/subscription | Continuous data protection | Journal-based any-second rewind

Why it earns 3: Zerto’s continuous journal lets you rewind to seconds before encryption began an RPO class snapshots can’t touch.

For revenue-critical applications where losing four hours of transactions is its own disaster, journal-based recovery is the difference-maker, now under HPE’s umbrella.

Pros: Seconds-level RPO; fast failover orchestration; encryption-detection triggers.

Cons: Journal economics scope it to tier-1 apps.

Bottom line: Rewind the tape to the second before impact.

4. Cohesity — Best Snapshot Threat Analytics

Snapshot: Quote | Threat scanning + classification on backup data | Veritas-merged vendor

Why it earns 4: Cohesity turned the backup corpus into a hunting ground threat scanning + classification on backup data, IOC scanning, ML anomaly detection, and classification over snapshots so clean-point selection is evidence-driven. Post-Veritas-merger scale broadens reach; roadmap diligence applies.

Pros: Strong threat analytics on snapshots; cyber-vault options.

Cons: Post-merger portfolio clarity.

Bottom line: Hunt the attacker inside your backups.

5. Commvault — Best Cleanroom Recovery

Snapshot: Subscription | Cleanroom recovery environments | Threat scanning + deception sensors

Why it earns 5: Commvault operationalized the step most programs improvise: an isolated cleanroom where restores are staged, scanned, and validated before touching production paired with early-warning deception and threat scanning across its broad workload matrix.

Pros: Cleanroom as product, not project; coverage depth.

Cons: Platform complexity reputation.

Bottom line: Rebuild in quarantine, then promote with confidence.

6. Druva — Best SaaS-Isolated Recovery

Snapshot: Per-workload SaaS | Backup estate outside your blast radius | Curated snapshots + quarantine

Why it earns 6: Druva’s recovery advantage is architectural: the backup platform lives in its cloud, not your compromised network, so the attacker who owns your domain can’t reach it.

Curated clean snapshots, quarantine, and accelerated-response tooling ride on that isolation.

Pros: Blast-radius isolation by design; zero recovery infrastructure to rebuild.

Cons: Massive on-prem restores bound by bandwidth planning.

Bottom line: Recovery capacity the attacker never touched.

7. Dell — Best Vault-Based Recovery

Snapshot: Quote | PowerProtect Cyber Recovery vault + CyberSense analytics

Why it earns 7: Dell’s vault pattern air-gapped copies analyzed by PowerProtect Cyber Recovery vault + CyberSense analytics gives boards and regulators a recovery story they can diagram: a sealed room of known-good data, scanned for corruption, ready for staged rebuild.

Pros: Mature air-gap architecture; integrity analytics; auditor-legible design.

Cons: Infrastructure-heavy; vault sizing discipline required.

Bottom line: The sealed-vault recovery pattern, productized.

8. IBM FlashSystem — Best Array-Speed Restores

Snapshot: Array-based | Safeguarded Copy immutable snapshots | Fast storage-level recovery

Why it earns 8: When ransomware strikes and terabytes of data need restoring, IBM FlashSystem helps businesses recover quickly using Safeguarded Copy.

Its protected snapshots cannot be modified or deleted through normal host access, even if production systems are compromised.

Storage-level recovery reduces dependence on slower traditional backup restores, making it a strong recovery layer for critical enterprise workloads.

Pros: Protected immutable snapshots; fast storage-level recovery; strong ransomware resilience.

Cons: Requires compatible IBM FlashSystem infrastructure; not a complete ransomware recovery platform.

Bottom line: Fast, protected recovery built directly into enterprise storage.

9. Acronis — Best SMB Recovery Blend

Snapshot: Published tiers | One-click recovery + active anti-ransomware | MSP-aligned

Why it earns 9: For SMBs and MSPs, Acronis compresses the whole cycle one-click recovery + active anti-ransomware that halts encryption, then one-click full-image recovery into one agent at published prices, which is the right shape when there’s no recovery team, just a Tuesday.

Pros: Integrated prevent+recover; accessible pricing; MSP tooling.

Cons: Enterprise orchestration depth limited.

Bottom line: The small-team recovery answer that actually gets deployed.

10. Index Engines — Best Independent Integrity Verification

Snapshot: Quote/OEM | CyberSense analytics | Validates backups across vendors

Why it earns 10: Index Engines plays referee: its CyberSense engine (also OEM’d in Dell’s vault) inspects backup content for corruption patterns with high published accuracy claims, independently of whichever backup vendor made the copies the second opinion a recovery decision deserves.

Pros: Vendor-independent integrity verdicts; deep content inspection.

Cons: Analytics layer, not a restore engine.

Bottom line: Proof your “clean” point is actually clean.

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Script the Worst Tuesday, Then Time It

Buy for the sequence, not the features: detection flags encryption → analytics identify the last clean point → integrity verification proves it → restores stage in isolation → validated workloads promote to production.

Walk every finalist through that exact sequence on your estate and demand timings.

Tier your applications first journal-based CDP (Zerto-class) for the revenue tier, snapshot platforms for the bulk, array-speed layers (Pure-class) where volume dominates.

Insist on immutability that survives stolen admin credentials, and add independent verification (Index Engines-class) if a wrong clean-point call would be existential. Then rehearse twice a year with the real on-call roster; the plan that lives in a PDF recovers nothing.

FAQs

What is the best ransomware recovery solution in 2026? Rubrik ranks 1 for clean-point intelligence, Veeam for verified restores across the broadest estates, and HPE Zerto for seconds-level rewind on tier-1 applications with Commvault’s cleanroom and Dell’s vault leading their patterns.

How is this different from the best backup solution? Backup rankings weigh protection breadth and operations; recovery rankings weigh the attack day clean-point identification, verification, and hours-to-business. Strong vendors appear on both lists for different reasons.

What’s a clean restore point and why is it hard? The last snapshot before attacker activity hard because dwell time means the attacker predates the encryption event, so you need analytics on backup history, not just timestamps.

How do you avoid restoring the infection? Stage restores in an isolated clean room, scan with independent analytics, rotate credentials before promotion, and never restore identity systems first without forensic validation.

What RPO should we target? Tier it: seconds (CDP) for revenue-critical transactions, hours (snapshots) for the bulk estate. Uniform RPO targets overspend on the many and underprotect the few.

Verdict

Rubrik tells you where clean lives, Veeam proves restores before you bet on them, Zerto rewinds the seconds that matter, and Index Engines referees everyone’s claims rank your finalists by stopwatch on your own worst-Tuesday script, because recovery is the one control whose demo is the incident.
