articles.title: StealC Malware Returns as New Stadia RAT to Steal Passwords and Secretly Control Windows PCs
articles.description:
The seller behind StealC has returned with Stadia, a Windows remote access trojan that combines password theft with hidden desktop control. Advertised on October 16, 2026, the malware expands beyond stealing data, allowing criminals to run commands, browse files, manage processes, and load more malicious software. The return follows June’s Operation Endgame disruption. Authorities seized […]

The post StealC Malware Returns as New Stadia RAT to Steal Passwords and Secretly Control Windows PCs appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The seller behind StealC has returned with Stadia, a Windows remote access trojan that combines password theft with hidden desktop control.

Advertised on October 16, 2026, the malware expands beyond stealing data, allowing criminals to run commands, browse files, manage processes, and load more malicious software.

The return follows June’s Operation Endgame disruption. Authorities seized 326 servers and 142 domains, according to Varonis.

Although the earlier StealC infrastructure takedown disrupted the criminal service, its surviving code gave the seller a foundation for rebuilding under a new name.

Researchers from Varonis Threat Labs identified Stadia’s connection to StealC after obtaining a build, examining its code, and testing its web panel against their own Windows machine.

Their technical analysis of Stadia found an embedded browser encryption helper shared byte for byte with StealC 3.5, providing direct evidence of code reuse.

StealC Malware Returns as New Stadia RAT

Stadia brings together six modules: a stealer, hidden desktop access, a remote command shell, a loader, a file explorer, and a process manager.

Hidden Virtual Network Computing, or HVNC, lets an operator work inside a separate desktop that the victim cannot see. The file tools support uploads, downloads, and execution.

The seller advertises collection from more than 50 browsers, 120 cryptocurrency extensions, and 50 desktop wallets. Targets also include messaging apps, gaming sessions, email clients, and VPN software.

Similar combinations appear in Dolphin X credential theft coverage, where stolen browser data and remote access create risks beyond individual account losses.

Monthly subscriptions cost $300 for Basic, $550 for Team, and $900 for Pro. Only Pro includes all six modules. Former StealC customers receive a free Pro month, helping the seller attract buyers whose previous infrastructure disappeared. The tested panel and agent both reported version 1.1.2.

How Stadia Hides and Communicates

The examined sample is an unsigned, 560,128-byte, 32-bit Windows executable built with Microsoft Visual C++. It hides important strings using RC4 encryption and Base64 encoding, while resolving most Windows functions during execution.

It also exits when certain Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Kazakh, or Uzbek language settings are detected. Installation creates a random folder beneath Windows’ shared application-data directory and uses a filename resembling legitimate software.

A hidden scheduled task runs at logon and every 15 minutes. With elevated permissions, Stadia also adds its installation folder to Microsoft Defender exclusions through PowerShell.

For browser theft, an unsigned process starts Chrome, Edge, or Brave in a suspended state and injects roughly 26 KB of code. A temporary text file briefly holds the recovered browser encryption key before deletion.

Related ChonkyChicken browser credential attacks show why protected browser storage remains an important monitoring target. Stadia contacts three hard-coded servers over HTTP.

Its requests claim to contain JSON, but actually carry RC4-encrypted, Base64-encoded data. Defenders should investigate this mismatch alongside suspicious browser injection, hidden tasks, and new antivirus exclusions.

Varonis warns that server addresses and keys change between builds, making behavior-based detection more durable than static blocking alone. The report does not establish an initial delivery method or independently verified infection count.

articles.description:
Public proof-of-concept code for two critical PHP vulnerabilities is now available, and attackers have tried to use the flaws to deploy botnet malware. Known together as PHP2Shell, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 both carry a CVSS severity score of 9.2 and can allow attackers to run code without logging in. However, attempted exploitation must not be confused […]

The post Critical PHP2Shell Exploit Code Goes Public as Hackers Attempt to Deploy Botnet Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Public proof-of-concept code for two critical PHP vulnerabilities is now available, and attackers have tried to use the flaws to deploy botnet malware.

Known together as PHP2Shell, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 both carry a CVSS severity score of 9.2 and can allow attackers to run code without logging in.

However, attempted exploitation must not be confused with a confirmed breach. In its latest correction, issued on October 22 at 21:21 UTC, Sophos said its customer data showed scanning and a small number of failed exploit attempts.

It found no evidence of a successful compromise through these vulnerabilities. Researchers from Sophos identified the intended payload as Potassium, a likely Mirai botnet variant. Security controls blocked the attempt, so the malware was not delivered.

Analysis of the sample nevertheless showed a larger, updated version of the Mirai-derived threat seen earlier in 2026, with download and network disruption features.

The activity follows earlier PHP2Shell targeting before patches became public. Reporting on PHP attacks before patching describes Amazon observations dating to October 17, four days before the fixes.

Those findings underline why defenders should review older logs, while keeping attempted attacks separate from proven code execution on real servers.

Critical PHP2Shell Exploit Code Goes Public

PHP released security updates on October 21. The affected software includes PHP installations serving web requests through PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed.

The Dutch National Cyber Security Centre notes that Apache mod_php carries the highest risk because exploitation can occur before application code starts running.

The flaws involve different failures in how PHP handles memory and request data. CVE-2026-109618 can corrupt memory during request cleanup after an out-of-memory condition.

CVE-2026-109619 concerns old request data left in shared internal state, which a later request handled by the same worker can reuse.

These weaknesses can expose more than a single website. Products that bundle PHP, including management interfaces and network appliances, may also need updates from their suppliers.

Administrators should therefore check the runtime used by each service, rather than relying only on the PHP version shown by a command-line check.

Public exploit code does not mean every vulnerable server can be compromised reliably. Sophos said its own research team found working exploitation difficult, even with AI support.

Earlier Cloudflare PHP attack coverage also shows why web application firewall rules are a temporary safeguard, not a replacement for updates.

Potassium Botnet Payload Examined

The blocked traffic included a scanning-related User-Agent, a multipart boundary, and a distinct POST request pattern. Sophos published a temporary file path and an execution command as related indicators.

Since its earlier success claim was withdrawn, those details should not be presented as proof that customer systems ran the payload.

Sample analysis showed that Potassium resolves an encrypted command-and-control address and makes an HTTP request. It checks for a successful HTTP 200 response and verifies that the returned file begins with Linux ELF magic bytes.

That check shows the downloader expects another Linux executable, rather than ordinary web content. The sample also supports hostname lookup and fallback resolution through public DNS services.

Those public services are not malicious indicators by themselves. Like other Mirai-based malware, Potassium can launch distributed denial-of-service attacks, using compromised machines to flood targets with traffic.

Separate RondoDoX botnet exploit activity illustrates similar interest in turning exposed application servers into botnet resources.

Organizations should update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, or install an approved vendor backport. Restarting affected services and checking the active workers helps ensure the patched code is actually in use.

Bundled runtimes, containers, and appliances need separate checks because updating one host package may leave other copies unchanged.

Sophos has added firewall and endpoint intrusion prevention signatures alongside existing detection rules. Defenders should keep these protections current, but assess alerts against process and network evidence.

A blocked request alone cannot show whether another request succeeded. Equally, a public exploit demonstration does not prove that the same code works against a production system with different settings, dependencies, or worker process behavior.

Where patching cannot happen immediately, Sophos recommends considering removal of exposed PHP systems from the internet or placing them behind network-level authentication.

Teams should monitor unusual processes, unexpected outbound connections, and suspicious web requests. Temporary settings and firewall signatures can reduce exposure, but they do not fully fix both flaws.

articles.title: Hackers Use New BlackX Bootkit to Bypass Windows Secure Boot on Fully Patched Systems
articles.description:
A new UEFI bootkit called BlackX has been used in cyberespionage attacks against diplomatic organizations in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan. The malware targets Secure Boot, a feature designed to help stop untrusted software from running before Windows starts. Researchers say the infected computers had received Windows updates, but a key Secure Boot protection had not […]

The post Hackers Use New BlackX Bootkit to Bypass Windows Secure Boot on Fully Patched Systems appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new UEFI bootkit called BlackX has been used in cyberespionage attacks against diplomatic organizations in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan.

The malware targets Secure Boot, a feature designed to help stop untrusted software from running before Windows starts.

Researchers say the infected computers had received Windows updates, but a key Secure Boot protection had not been fully applied.

Securelist analysts reported the findings on October 22, 2026. They say BlackX uses Baton Drop, a vulnerability tracked as CVE-2022-21894, and shares parts of its design with the BlackLotus bootkit.

The findings show why an installed update does not always mean that the protection it is meant to provide has been fully activated. Securelist’s BlackX report describes the malware and the campaign in detail.

BlackX is installed after attackers have already gained access to a victim’s network and administrator-level rights. Its installer, inst.exe, works with an encrypted file named PVMDIJGKAX2, which contains components needed to install the malware.

Securelist says this design can make it harder for incident responders to recover all the bootkit’s parts from the installer alone. The bootkit uses Baton Drop to load attacker-controlled EFI files and interfere with Secure Boot.

EFI files run during the computer’s startup process, before Windows loads. By gaining a place in that early sequence, a bootkit can give malicious code a chance to run before many operating-system security tools are active.

Hackers Use New BlackX Bootkit

Readers can learn more about related boot-time risks in this Cybersecurity News report on managing UEFI Secure Boot settings.

Securelist says the campaign’s kernel driver attempts to weaken security tools by disrupting process, thread, and registry callbacks, and by interfering with Event Tracing for Windows (ETW), which software can use to collect system activity.

It also tries to hide its files: when certain file requests are made, the driver reportedly returns a handle to the legitimate calc.exe process instead of to the requested malicious file.

The bootkit also delivers user-mode malware for espionage. One payload is a remote-access Trojan that can load additional .NET code and use Google Drive, OneDrive, or Yandex.Disk for command-and-control communication.

Another, named OxiDLLRunner by the researchers, decrypts a file called v8_context_snapshot.bin and runs a Rust payload that contacts a reported command-and-control domain.

The report links the activity to APT41 with medium confidence, based on overlaps with previously reported activity and shared technical details. That assessment is not definitive attribution.

Why patched systems were still at risk

The issue was not simply that the targeted computers lacked Windows updates. Securelist says the protection against Baton Drop depends on revoking trust in the “Windows Production PCA 2011” certificate used to sign vulnerable UEFI components.

Installing an update and applying that revocation are separate steps in the process described by the researchers. Microsoft’s guidance for CVE-2023-24932 also describes multiple steps for deploying Secure Boot protections, including updating certificates, boot managers, and the UEFI revocation list.

Its instructions warn that blocking older boot components can affect recovery media and other boot options, so administrators should test changes and prepare recovery options before applying them broadly. See Microsoft’s Secure Boot revocation guidance.

The distinction matters because Windows may report that updates are installed even when the firmware’s forbidden-signature list has not yet been updated as intended.

Securelist reported that the certificate’s expiration on October 19, 2026, did not by itself stop vulnerable binaries from loading; the certificate must be blocked by the relevant revocation mechanism.

Administrators should therefore verify their devices’ Secure Boot configuration and revocation status, following Microsoft’s current instructions and accounting for their organization’s boot and recovery needs.

BlackX is not the first bootkit story to raise questions about trust in old boot components. Cybersecurity News has previously covered BlackLotus and how a downgrade technique could leave a Windows device exposed despite an up-to-date status.

That background helps explain why Secure Boot protection depends on more than the visible update state of Windows. The main lesson for defenders is to confirm that Secure Boot protections are active in firmware, not only that Windows updates have been installed.

Organizations should review Microsoft’s deployment guidance, verify that the necessary revocations have taken effect, and check boot and recovery media for compatibility.

Since BlackX was installed after attackers obtained administrator access, teams should also investigate suspicious administrative activity and boot-related changes, and review endpoint alerts for signs that security monitoring has been tampered with.

articles.description:
State Bank of India (SBI) has individually notified customers whose information was identified in a recent cyber incident, sending alerts through email and WhatsApp. In its latest advisory on October 23, the bank said customer account balances and funds remain safe while investigators examine the suspected exposure of personal information found on the dark web. […]

The post SBI Notifies Customers Impacted by the Recent Cyber Incident appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
State Bank of India (SBI) has individually notified customers whose information was identified in a recent cyber incident, sending alerts through email and WhatsApp.

In its latest advisory on October 23, the bank said customer account balances and funds remain safe while investigators examine the suspected exposure of personal information found on the dark web.

The update shifts the bank’s response from an initial public disclosure to direct communication with customers. According to The Economic Times, SBI said it had informed all customers whose data was identified as involved.

The bank also warned users to stay alert for suspicious calls, messages, and emails, and never share passwords, PINs, or one-time passwords.

SBI’s preliminary review examined approximately 375,000 records available on the dark web and identified 3,897 customer records containing personally identifiable information.

These figures represent different measures. The larger number describes the records reviewed, not a confirmed count of affected SBI customers or compromised bank accounts.

SBI Notifies Customers Impacted By Cyber Incident

The information reportedly included names, registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, email addresses and home addresses. Other fields included gender, branch details, Customer Information File identifiers, and information linked to loan inquiries and lead records. These details can identify customers and provide context about their banking relationships.

As covered in Cybersecurity News’ earlier report on the SBI data loss incident, the disclosure did not establish how the information was obtained.

It also did not confirm that attackers had entered SBI’s core banking systems. No publicly identified entry point, exploited software flaw, or malware family explained the incident.

SBI received alerts on October 16 from its threat intelligence service provider, the Defense Cyber Agency, and the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, known as CERT-In.

The bank activated its incident response and containment procedures and appointed an independent cybersecurity agency impaneled with CERT-In to investigate.

Investigators are examining the authenticity, source and extent of the exposed information. SBI has said the incident caused no material impact on its core operations, financial performance or business continuity. Banking services continued without disruption, according to the bank’s disclosure.

An earlier unverified claim about an SBI data breach alleged that customer records and banking documents had been posted online. Those allegations should remain separate from SBI’s confirmed findings while the investigation continues.

Personal data exposure does not automatically mean an account has been taken over. Available reporting does not establish that passwords, PINs, OTPs, or transaction credentials were compromised. However, exposed contact and loan details could help criminals create convincing messages that appear to come from the bank.

Customers should verify unexpected notifications through official banking channels rather than trust a message because it contains accurate personal details. They should avoid unfamiliar links and check statements for unauthorized transactions.

SBI’s official cybersecurity guidance lists report.phishing@sbi.co.in for reporting cyber incidents and directs users to India’s cybercrime helpline, 1930. The bank’s latest warning stresses that customers must never disclose authentication codes or banking passwords to anyone.

The post Top 10 Best Email Encryption Services in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Email encryption has a usability paradox: the strongest cryptography loses to the recipient who gives up at the portal login and asks for the file “some other way.”

The 2026 winners solve for both ends sender-side automation (policies, DLP triggers, one-click protect) and recipient experiences that don’t require a manual.

We scored ten services on exactly that trade, plus control depth (expiry, revoke, audit) and compliance evidence.

Virtru takes 1; Microsoft Purview and Proofpoint complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Virtru the lowest-friction path to encrypted mail recipients actually open.

• Podium: Virtru (recipient experience), Purview Message Encryption (M365 gravity), Proofpoint (gateway-policy muscle).

• Consolidation flag: Zix, the compliance-encryption veteran, now lives inside OpenText renewal diligence applies.

• Healthcare lane: Paubox’s no-portal delivery is the HIPAA-workflow standout.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation: recipient friction (no-portal/no-account paths), policy automation (DLP-triggered, content-aware encryption), sender controls (expiry, revoke, disable-forward, audit), compliance evidence (HIPAA/GDPR-class), platform fit, and pricing structure.

No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Weights: recipient friction 30%, policy automation 25%, sender controls 20%, compliance evidence 15%, pricing clarity 10%.

The 2026 Email Encryption Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Virtru — Best Recipient Experience

Snapshot: Published tiers | Gmail/Outlook-native | TDF open standard | Expiry, revoke, watermark

Why it earns 1: Virtru wins where encryption actually fails the recipient: external parties open protected messages in a browser without accounts, plugins, or password ping-pong, while senders get one-click protection plus expiry, revocation, disable-forward, and DLP-triggered automation.

Built on the open Trusted Data Format rather than a proprietary silo, it deploys in days on Gmail or M365 and users keep using it, which is the entire game.

Pros: Lowest recipient friction in the lane; strong sender controls; fast deployment; open standard.

Cons: Gateway-class policy breadth is not the aim.

Bottom line: Encryption people don’t route around.

2. Microsoft Purview Message Encryption — Best M365-Native

Snapshot: E3/E5-bundled | Label and rule-driven | Office-native reading experience

Why it earns 2: For M365 estates, Purview Message Encryption is capability already licensed: encryption triggered by sensitivity labels and transport rules, seamless reading inside the Microsoft world, and a tolerable one-time-passcode path outside it.

Configure this floor before paying anyone then buy only for the friction and control gaps you can still name.

Pros: Bundle economics; label-driven automation; in-ecosystem seamlessness.

Cons: External-recipient OTP flow is serviceable, not delightful; advanced controls fragment across SKUs.

Bottom line: The floor every M365 tenant should fully enable.

3. Proofpoint — Best Gateway-Policy Encryption

Snapshot: Quote/tiered | Encryption inside the leading SEG | Content-aware triggers

Why it earns 3: Proofpoint encrypts as a function of the gateway that already reads every outbound message: DLP dictionaries, smart identifiers, and policy routes trigger encryption automatically no user decisions required with enterprise reporting attached.

For organizations that want encryption as enforced policy rather than user choice, this leading SEG is the lane’s anchor.

Pros: Policy automation depth; DLP integration; enterprise reporting.

Cons: Portal-based recipient experience; platform cost.

Bottom line: Encryption as outbound policy, enforced by the gateway.

4. Paubox — Best No-Portal HIPAA Delivery

Snapshot: Published tiers | TLS-delivered, portal-free | HIPAA-focused, BAA included

Why it earns 4: Paubox’s bet: encrypted email should land in the recipient’s normal inbox, readable like any message no portal, no passcode with secure fallback only when TLS can’t be verified.

For healthcare workflows where patients and partners won’t tolerate portals, that design plus HIPAA-focused, BAA included protections made it the clinic-to-enterprise favorite.

Pros: Zero recipient friction; HIPAA-purposed with BAA; honest fallback design.

Cons: Sender-side controls (revoke/expiry) lighter than rights-based rivals.

Bottom line: HIPAA email that reads like email.

5. Mimecast — Best Suite-Integrated Secure Messaging

Snapshot: Tiered | Secure Messaging inside the email-security suite | Policy-driven

Why it earns 5: Mimecast folds Secure Messaging inside the email-security suite already handling hygiene, continuity, and archiving one admin plane, policy-triggered protection, and a portal flow recipients see across thousands of Mimecast-protected brands. Consolidation value for its large installed base.

Pros: Suite consolidation; policy automation; familiar at scale.

Cons: Portal experience; deepest value only inside the suite.

Bottom line: The suite shop’s encryption checkbox, competently done.

6. Cisco Secure Email Encryption — Best Network-Suite Encryption

Snapshot: Licensed | ESA/CES-integrated encryption service | Enterprise policy ties

Why it earns 6: Cisco’s encryption service rides its email-security estate with an ESA/CES-integrated encryption service, registered-envelope delivery, policy triggers, and the procurement comfort of the networking incumbent a rational pick where Cisco already owns the mail path.

Pros: Cisco-estate integration; enterprise procurement fit.

Cons: Envelope/portal recipient flow; innovation pace.

Bottom line: The Cisco estate’s native encryption lane.

7. Echoworx — Best Encryption-Delivery Specialist

Snapshot: Quote | Encryption-only focus | Multiple delivery methods per recipient

Why it earns 7: Echoworx does one thing with unusual care: delivery-method intelligence that picks the best path per recipient TLS, portal, attachment, certificate with strong branding control and multi-language support, which is why banks and insurers white-label it.

Pros: Delivery-method flexibility; white-label depth; specialist focus.

Cons: Point solution in a suite-consolidating market.

Bottom line: The delivery-intelligence specialist behind big brands.

8. OpenText (Zix) — Best Compliance-Lineage Encryption

Snapshot: Tiered | Zix heritage | Transparent Zix-to-Zix community delivery

Why it earns 8: Zix built the healthcare/finance compliance-encryption franchise including its signature transparent delivery between Zix-community members and now operates inside OpenText’s portfolio.

The installed base is vast; buyers should confirm roadmap investment and packaging under OpenText at renewal.

Pros: Compliance pedigree; community transparent delivery; large regulated base.

Cons: Portfolio-era roadmap diligence.

Bottom line: The compliance veteran, now under a bigger roof.

9. Trend Micro — Best Bundled Email-Security Encryption

Snapshot: Bundled/tiered | Encryption within email security | Hosted key service

Why it earns 9: Trend delivers policy-triggered encryption as part of its email-security bundle a pragmatic checkbox for estates already standardized on Trend’s stack rather than a destination purchase.

Pros: Bundle convenience; policy triggers.

Cons: Not the lane’s innovation driver.

Bottom line: Fine where Trend already guards the mail.

10. Barracuda — Best SMB-Bundle Encryption

Snapshot: Published bundles | Encryption inside Email Protection plans | SMB-friendly

Why it earns 10: Barracuda includes encryption in SMB-priced email-protection bundles simple policies, simple portal, one invoice the honest answer for small teams who need the checkbox met without an encryption project.

Pros: SMB pricing and simplicity.

Cons: Control depth and recipient polish are basic.

Bottom line: The small-business checkbox, affordably ticked.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Send One Message to Your Hardest Recipient

Run the only test that predicts adoption: send an encrypted message to a real external recipient the 70-year-old patient, the counterparty on Gmail, the vendor on Exchange 2016 and count their clicks to reading it.

More than two, and your users will eventually bypass the tool. Configure your bundle floor first (Purview or Workspace rules), then buy for named gaps: recipient friction (Virtru/Paubox-class), gateway-grade policy enforcement (Proofpoint-class), or white-label delivery (Echoworx-class).

Make encryption automatic DLP and label triggers, never user memory because the breach email is always the one someone forgot to protect.

Healthcare: insist on the BAA and test the patient-reply path, not just outbound. And at Zix renewals, price the OpenText-era roadmap against the switching cost honestly.

FAQs

What is the best email encryption service in 2026? Virtru ranks 1 for recipient experience plus sender controls, Microsoft Purview for M365-bundled automation, and Proofpoint for gateway-enforced policy with Paubox the HIPAA no-portal standout.

Is TLS enough for email encryption? Opportunistic TLS protects most hops but fails silently and proves nothing per-message. Compliance-grade programs need enforced encryption with fallback and evidence which is precisely what this category sells.

Do recipients need accounts to read encrypted mail? Not with the leaders: Virtru reads in-browser, Paubox lands inbox-native, Zix is transparent in-community. Portal-and-password flows are the adoption tax to minimize.

What makes email encryption HIPAA-compliant? A BAA with the vendor, enforced encryption policies, audit trails, and workflow fit so staff actually use it. The tool is necessary; the program makes it compliant.

Can I revoke an email after sending? With rights-based services (Virtru-class, Purview in-ecosystem), yes access checks happen at open, so you can kill it after delivery. Gateway/portal models vary; test it before relying on it.

Verdict

Virtru proved usable encryption wins, Purview made the floor nearly free for M365 shops, Proofpoint enforces protection nobody has to remember, and Paubox made HIPAA mail read like mail pick by your hardest recipient’s click count, automate the trigger, and let the bundle-vs-gap math decide the invoice.

The post Top 9 Best Managed File Transfer (MFT) Solutions in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
No category has been breached more publicly this decade than managed file transfer mass-exploitation campaigns against MFT products turned quiet integration plumbing into board-level risk, and the 2023–2024 waves rewrote the buying criteria.

In 2026 you evaluate an MFT vendor’s security engineering exposure architecture, patch velocity, hardening posture before its scheduler.

Our sheet listed ten rows, but two of them (GoAnywhere and Globalscape) are both Fortra products, so this is an honest Top 9 vendors.

Axway takes 1; IBM Sterling and Progress MOVEit complete a podium where resilience history is part of the score.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Axway enterprise MFT depth with a security-architecture story intact.

• Podium: Axway (enterprise depth), IBM Sterling (B2B backbone scale), Progress MOVEit (hardened survivor with rebuilt posture).

• Consolidation note: Fortra owns both GoAnywhere and Globalscape EFT one vendor, two products; we rank the vendor once.

• New buying criterion: demand the vendor’s exploitation history, patch SLAs, and secure-deployment reference architecture in writing.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation: security architecture and track record (internet-exposure design, hardening guidance, disclosure/patch velocity), automation and orchestration depth, B2B protocol breadth (SFTP/AS2/AS4/APIs), compliance evidence, operational scale, and pricing structure.

No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Weights: security posture 30%, automation depth 25%, protocol/B2B breadth 20%, operational scale 15%, pricing clarity 10%.

The 2026 MFT Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Axway — Best Enterprise MFT Depth

Snapshot: Quote | Managed File Transfer + Amplify platform | Governance at financial-services scale

Why it earns 1: Axway runs the transfer backbones of banks and logistics giants with central governance over thousands of flows, strong identity integration, and an API-management adjacency that modernizes B2B patterns instead of embalming them while keeping a security-architecture reputation that survived the category’s worst years intact.

Pros: Governance at scale; API/MFT convergence; enterprise references.

Cons: Enterprise weight; quote-only economics.

Bottom line: The backbone-grade incumbent still earning the position.

2. IBM (Sterling) — Best B2B Backbone Scale

Snapshot: Quote | Sterling File Gateway/Connect:Direct | Decades of mission-critical transfer

Why it earns 2: When the requirement is millions of files across thousands of partners with mainframe-to-cloud reach, Sterling’s File Gateway and Connect:Direct lineage remains the reference: high-assurance point-to-point transfer, deep partner-community management, and the operational hardening of forty years in production.

Pros: Unmatched scale pedigree; Connect:Direct assurance; partner-management depth.

Cons: Modernization effort and cost; skills scarcity.

Bottom line: The heavyweight for estates where failure isn’t survivable.

3. Progress (MOVEit) — Hardened Survivor, Rebuilt Posture

Snapshot: Licensed/quote | MOVEit Transfer/Automation | Post-2023 security overhaul

Why it earns 3: MOVEit is the category’s cautionary tale and its stress test: the 2023 mass exploitation forced a security rebuild expanded testing, hardening guidance, bounty and disclosure investment that buyers should verify rather than assume, but the product’s automation depth and compliance toolkit remain first-rank. We rank it on capability plus demonstrated remediation, with the diligence burden stated plainly.

Pros: Automation and reporting depth; large install base; visible post-incident investment.

Cons: Breach history requires explicit diligence; internet-exposure discipline mandatory.

Bottom line: Strong product make the rebuilt posture prove itself in writing.

4. Fortra (GoAnywhere + Globalscape EFT) — Broadest Portfolio, One Vendor

Snapshot: Licensed/quote | Two MFT lines under one roof | Sheet listed both; we count one vendor

Why it earns 4: Fortra owns two of the market’s best-known products GoAnywhere’s automation-rich platform and Globalscape EFT’s Windows-centric depth so our ten-row sheet yields nine vendors.

GoAnywhere’s own 2023 exploitation means the same diligence standard as MOVEit applies: demand patch-velocity evidence and the zero-exposure reference architecture. Portfolio overlap also makes roadmap questions fair game at renewal.

Pros: Two mature products; strong automation (GoAnywhere); portfolio flexibility.

Cons: Exploitation history (GoAnywhere) and two-product roadmap clarity.

Bottom line: One vendor, two products — pick the line, and get the roadmap in writing.

5. Cleo — Best Ecosystem-Integration MFT

Snapshot: Subscription/quote | Cleo Integration Cloud | MFT fused with EDI/API integration

Why it earns 5: Cleo’s bet is that transfers are integrations: its Integration Cloud unifies MFT, EDI, and API flows with end-to-end visibility into the business transaction, not just the file hop the right shape for supply-chain estates where a late file is a late shipment.

Its own 2024 exploitation episode requires the same posture diligence as its peers.

Pros: Transaction-level visibility; EDI/API convergence; supply-chain fit.

Cons: Posture diligence applies here too.

Bottom line: MFT that understands the business document inside the file.

6. SEEBURGER — Best Integration-Suite MFT

Snapshot: Quote | BIS platform | MFT as one engine of a B2B/EDI/API suite

Why it earns 6: SEEBURGER delivers MFT inside its Business Integration Suite one platform spanning EDI, API, and IoT flows with German-engineering governance compelling where the enterprise wants a single integration estate rather than a standalone transfer tool.

Pros: True suite consolidation; strong European/manufacturing base.

Cons: Suite commitment is the price of entry.

Bottom line: For estates consolidating all integration, not just transfers.

7. Kiteworks — Best Governed-Exchange MFT

Snapshot: Quote | MFT inside the private content network | Hardened virtual appliance

Why it earns 7: Kiteworks folds MFT into its governed exchange plane the same policy, audit, and hardened virtual appliance architecture covering email and sharing attractive when the driver is provable third-party-risk governance across every channel rather than scheduler horsepower.

Pros: One audit plane across channels; hardened-deployment design.

Cons: Deep legacy-B2B protocol estates may outgrow it.

Bottom line: MFT as evidence, not just movement.

8. Redwood (JSCAPE) — Best Platform-Agnostic Value

Snapshot: Licensed/quote | JSCAPE MFT Server | Any-platform deployment, now under Redwood

Why it earns 8: JSCAPE’s platform-agnostic server (Windows/Linux/cloud, broad protocol support, clustering) now rides Redwood’s automation ecosystem a pragmatic mid-enterprise choice, with Redwood-era packaging worth confirming.

Pros: Deployment flexibility; protocol breadth; automation-ecosystem ties.

Cons: Brand transition diligence.

Bottom line: Flexible, sensible, and now part of an automation house.

9. Coviant (Diplomat) — Best Focused SFTP Automation Value

Snapshot: Published tiers | Diplomat MFT | PGP-automation specialist

Why it earns 9: Coviant’s Diplomat does the unglamorous core scheduled SFTP with airtight PGP key handling and alerting at published prices and small-team complexity, the honest answer when you need reliable encrypted transfers, not a B2B integration estate.

Pros: Right-sized; strong PGP automation; transparent pricing.

Cons: Not aiming at partner-community scale.

Bottom line: The focused tool that does transfers well and stops there.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Interrogate the Posture Before the Scheduler

The category’s breach history writes your evaluation script. First, exposure architecture: no MFT admin interface internet-facing, ever demand the vendor’s zero-exposure reference design (gateway/proxy tier) and deploy it from day one.

Second, posture evidence: exploitation history handled, patch SLAs, time-to-patch track record for the last three CVEs, bounty program, hardening guide quality in writing, scored like a feature.

Third, operational resilience: can you patch within 24 hours of an advisory without breaking flows (staging environment, rollback plan)? Then and only then compare schedulers, protocol breadth, and partner onboarding.

Inventory your flows before shortlisting ten SFTP jobs point to Coviant/JSCAPE-class value; thousands of partner flows point to Axway/Sterling; EDI-entangled supply chains to Cleo/SEEBURGER; audit-plane governance to Kiteworks.

And wire MFT telemetry into the SOC: these systems are breach targets, so watch them like crown jewels, not plumbing.

FAQs

What is the best managed file transfer solution in 2026? Axway ranks 1 for enterprise depth with posture intact, IBM Sterling for backbone scale, and Progress MOVEit as the hardened survivor whose rebuilt security buyers should verify with Coviant and JSCAPE leading the value lanes.

Why only 9 vendors? Our source sheet listed GoAnywhere and Globalscape separately, but both are Fortra products one vendor, ranked once with both lines noted.

Is MOVEit safe to buy after 2023? The product remains capable and Progress has invested visibly in security since. Buy it the modern way: zero-exposure deployment, contractual patch SLAs, and your own 24-hour-patch capability.

MFT vs secure file sharing which do we need? MFT moves files between systems on schedules and triggers; sharing platforms serve humans collaborating. Most enterprises need both see our secure file sharing ranking for the human side.

What’s the single most important MFT security control? Architecture: no directly internet-exposed admin surface, a gateway tier in the DMZ, and SOC monitoring of the MFT estate itself. Most category breaches exploited exposed services.

Verdict

Axway and Sterling carry the backbones, MOVEit and GoAnywhere carry lessons the whole category paid for, and Cleo and SEEBURGER fold transfers into the integrations they really are buy the security architecture first, the scheduler second, and treat every MFT server as the crown-jewel target attackers already proved it is.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Critical Citrix NetScaler RCE Flaw to Deploy Web Shells and Malware
articles.description:
A critical vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway is being exploited to run commands on exposed appliances, install web shells and deliver malware. Tracked as CVE-2026-88771, the flaw allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute commands remotely. Citrix disclosed it on September 27, 2026, and confirmed exploitation of appliances that had not been protected […]

The post Hackers Exploit Critical Citrix NetScaler RCE Flaw to Deploy Web Shells and Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A critical vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway is being exploited to run commands on exposed appliances, install web shells and deliver malware.

Tracked as CVE-2026-88771, the flaw allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute commands remotely. Citrix disclosed it on September 27, 2026, and confirmed exploitation of appliances that had not been protected by an update.

The vulnerability is rated 9.8 under CVSS v3.1 and 9.5 under CVSS v4.0, according to the Zscaler ThreatLabz report. The activity is concerning because NetScaler devices often sit at the edge of company networks and handle remote access or application traffic.

A web shell can provide a way back into a compromised appliance, while a separate malware implant can give attackers another foothold.

The campaign also shows why applying a patch alone may not be enough: organizations need to check whether attackers already changed files, settings or system logs.

Researchers from Zscaler ThreatLabz identified a staged exploitation chain that used log poisoning, command execution, attempts to place web shells and delivery of a FreeBSD malware implant.

Their technical analysis of CVE-2026-88771 says the attackers first placed encoded content in web access logs, then sent crafted authentication requests designed to trigger a vulnerable diagnostic process.

Hackers Exploit Critical Citrix NetScaler RCE Flaw

In the observed activity, requests to common NetScaler web paths carried a distinctive “INDEX:” marker and encoded content in the User-Agent field.

These requests were intended to get attacker-controlled data written to access logs; the initial request did not itself run the full payload. Attackers then sent authentication requests containing text made to resemble a Packet Processing Engine failure message.

The vulnerable process, a Perl diagnostic script, later handled matching log entries. According to Zscaler, the script did not safely handle attacker-controlled characters in the forged message.

When the script processed a poisoned entry, appended commands could run with its privileges. This delayed method helps explain why a request that appears to be ordinary web or login traffic may be part of a larger attempt to compromise an appliance.

The observed payloads attempted to create web-accessible files, enable PHP or Perl handling in the web server, and install files named Nx_7508.php and Nx_7508.pl.

Researchers also saw attempts to download and run a 64-bit FreeBSD binary named kw2-freebsd-x64-s11. Zscaler reported that the download infrastructure had also appeared in activity targeting Magento and Adobe Commerce with CVE-2026-75650, known as StyleSmuggler.

That overlap is an investigative lead, not proof that the same threat actor carried out both campaigns. This is not the first time attackers have used NetScaler flaws to leave behind web shells.

Cyber Security News previously reported on web shells on hacked Citrix NetScalers and a separate campaign involving Citrix NetScaler zero-days and malware.

These earlier reports are useful context, but they concern different incidents and should not be treated as evidence that the same operators are responsible.

What organizations should do

Citrix’s fixed builds listed in the Zscaler report are NetScaler ADC and Gateway 14.1-73.46 or later, and 13.1-64.29 or later. The report also lists 14.1-73.46 FIPS or later for 14.1-FIPS, and 13.1.37.283 or later for 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP.

Administrators should verify the correct build for their product and upgrade promptly. Before updating, preserve relevant evidence where possible, including remote syslog data, technical support bundles and available core dumps.

Then review authentication and web access logs for suspicious “INDEX:” User-Agent values, forged “pitboss PPE” failure messages, unexpected requests to the paths listed below, and appliance-initiated connections to unfamiliar hosts.

Also inspect for unapproved web files, changed web-server settings and suspicious processes. If compromise is suspected, isolate the appliance while preserving evidence and rotate credentials, tokens and certificates it could access.

Patching prevents further exploitation of the flaw, but does not by itself remove an existing web shell or implant. Related coverage of another critical NetScaler flaw and previous NetScaler exploitation can help teams compare the current activity with earlier disclosures.

The weaknesses and campaigns differ, so responders should use the indicators below for this incident and check the relevant vendor guidance for each flaw.

articles.title: Hacker With Limited Skills Used DeepSeek AI to Breach Indian University and Steal Over 5,200 Records
articles.description:
A cybercriminal using the online handle BUGSTER used artificial intelligence tools to support attacks on Indian organizations, including two universities. In one confirmed intrusion, the attacker stole a MongoDB database containing more than 5,200 records, including personal information about students and staff, according to Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42. The researchers did not name the […]

The post Hacker With Limited Skills Used DeepSeek AI to Breach Indian University and Steal Over 5,200 Records appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A cybercriminal using the online handle BUGSTER used artificial intelligence tools to support attacks on Indian organizations, including two universities.

In one confirmed intrusion, the attacker stole a MongoDB database containing more than 5,200 records, including personal information about students and staff, according to Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42. The researchers did not name the universities.

The actor’s setup combined Hermes Agent, an AI assistant framework, with DeepSeek V4 as its reasoning model and Cursor as a coding tool.

Unit 42 said the attacker turned off safety controls and relied on AI-written scripts and reports. The case shows how AI can help a person with limited skills take on tasks that once demanded more experience, though it does not mean the model carried out the activity on its own.

Analysts from Unit 42 identified and investigated the activity by examining the operator’s environment, tools and records.

They found evidence of activity beyond the university intrusions, including credential theft, Wi-Fi password cracking, cryptocurrency research, and plans for phone-service fraud.

Hacker With Limited Skills Used DeepSeek AI

At one university, the actor used AI-assisted research to map an online education platform and its related services. The report described a WordPress site, a learning platform, a student portal and an administration dashboard.

The actor then used the information to try account passwords, and the tool identified one working login. Unit 42 did not say that this activity led to the theft of the 5,200 records; that database came from a separate university intrusion.

In the second case, the actor accessed a public university’s database with an administrator account protected by a weak password. The stolen MongoDB data included student records from diploma, undergraduate and postgraduate programs, as well as faculty information.

The actor’s records also showed details about parts of the university’s cloud and database setup. These incidents show why an exposed service or weak account can have serious effects, even without a newly discovered software flaw.

The activity described by Unit 42 relied on basic tools, information gathered about the targets and access to an administrator account.

Readers following DeepSeek-powered Hermes Agent attacks can compare this case with another report on AI-assisted activity involving the same tools.

AI supported work across several schemes

Unit 42 said the actor used AI-generated reports to organize research and produce scripts. Investigators also found a large credential-scanning toolkit designed to look for exposed secrets, such as cloud keys and private keys in files or logs.

This kind of information can give criminals access to services if an organization has left it unprotected. The actor also built AI profiles for separate tasks. One profile was used to seek advice about VoIP fraud, while another researched phone carriers.

Unit 42 found planning material but no call records or signs that the phone operation had become active. This distinction matters: the report documents preparation and research, not proof that the planned fraud was carried out.

Other activity included an automated process for trying to crack Wi-Fi passwords. Unit 42 said it required a device near the target networks to collect authentication data, suggesting the actor had local access to the locations.

The actor also collected information about large cryptocurrency holders, but researchers did not find evidence of follow-up activity against them.

Related reporting on DeepSeek safety research findings covers concerns about AI models producing harmful guidance. Unit 42’s findings add a different point: an attacker can combine an AI model with ordinary tools and weak account security to pursue several types of crime.

Universities and other organizations should review administrator accounts, remove weak or reused passwords, and require multi-factor authentication where possible.

They should also limit database access to approved systems and users, check internet-facing portals for unnecessary exposure, and monitor account activity for unusual login attempts or access to large sets of records.

Organizations should protect secrets such as API keys and cloud credentials by keeping them out of public files and logs. If a credential may have been exposed, teams should revoke or rotate it, then review access records for signs of misuse.

These steps address the security gaps described in the report; they do not depend on identifying a particular AI model. The activity also highlights the value of monitoring what AI agents can access.

If AI tools are used for legitimate work, organizations should limit their permissions, keep safety and approval controls enabled, and review their actions. The case is part of a wider set of reported concerns about AI-enabled cybercrime, including DeepSeek-powered credential theft activity.

articles.title: Oracle Issues Emergency Java Update for Critical 9.1 HTTPS Trust Vulnerability
articles.description:
Oracle has released an emergency Java security update to address CVE-2026-91403, a critical vulnerability affecting how Java applications trust digital certificates. Published on October 21, 2026, the alert assigns the flaw a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.1 and covers Oracle Java SE and GraalVM. The update blocks affected intermediate certificate authority certificates linked to eMudhra. […]

The post Oracle Issues Emergency Java Update for Critical 9.1 HTTPS Trust Vulnerability appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Oracle has released an emergency Java security update to address CVE-2026-91403, a critical vulnerability affecting how Java applications trust digital certificates. Published on October 21, 2026, the alert assigns the flaw a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.1 and covers Oracle Java SE and GraalVM. The update blocks affected intermediate certificate authority certificates linked to eMudhra.

According to Oracle’s security advisory, the issue affects the Java Secure Socket Extension, or JSSE, component. Oracle rates exploitation as low complexity, with no authentication or user interaction required. Successful attacks can expose or change sensitive data, although the risk matrix lists no availability impact.

The problem involves certificate chains that Java uses to decide whether a remote service is trusted. Red Hat explains that eMudhra issued intermediate certificates with weak private keys. An attacker positioned between a Java client and a server could use those weak keys to create certificates for arbitrary hostnames, making a malicious site appear trusted.

This undermines the identity checks behind HTTPS. Encryption alone cannot protect a connection when the client accepts an attacker’s certificate as valid. The fix therefore changes which certificates Java accepts, rather than removing HTTPS support or replacing the entire certificate system. Oracle’s update specifically distrusts the impacted intermediate certificates.

Affected Java and GraalVM Versions

Oracle lists Java SE 8u511, 8u511-perf, 11.0.33, 17.0.21, 21.0.13, 25.0.5, and 27.0.1 as affected. GraalVM for JDK 17.0.21 and 21.0.13, alongside GraalVM Enterprise Edition 21.3.20, are also included. Earlier releases may be vulnerable, but unsupported versions were not tested.

Oracle notes that affected APIs can be reached through services supplying data to JSSE. Its advisory also covers certain sandboxed Java Web Start applications and applets that load untrusted code. The announcement does not report confirmed attacks exploiting this vulnerability.

Oracle recommends installing the latest Java update or following its eMudhra mitigation instructions. Teams unable to update immediately can replace the local blocked.certs file with Oracle’s supplied version, preserving existing custom entries. Java 8 requires the replacement file to be named blacklisted.certs.

Alternatively, Oracle advises enabling TLS revocation checks using -Dcom.sun.net.ssl.checkRevocation=true and -Dcom.sun.security.enableCRLDP=true. For signed JAR verification on JDK 17 and later, it provides jarsigner -verify -revcheck -strict [SIGNED_JAR]. These are alternatives, not steps that must all be applied together.

The emergency alert follows Oracle’s wider patching efforts, including its September security update and August security patches. However, administrators should check this specific advisory rather than assume earlier updates cover the certificate issue. Oracle directs customers to its patch availability document for installation details and recommends moving unsupported deployments to supported releases.

This alleged data theft includes human resources records, training materials, and internal documents. However, the claims are unverified, and PwC has not yet responded. The group’s listing was reported on October 22, 2026. Hackmanac’s public alert […]

The post PwC Data Breach Claim – Everest Ransomware Group Claims to Have Stolen 590 GB of Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The Everest ransomware group claims to have stolen 590.69 GB of data from PwC, the global professional services firm. This alleged data theft includes human resources records, training materials, and internal documents. However, the claims are unverified, and PwC has not yet responded.

The group’s listing was reported on October 22, 2026. Hackmanac’s public alert described 108,426 files allegedly taken from internal HR and learning systems. Separately, CTIWatch’s victim tracker recorded PwC appearing on Everest’s leak site that day. These reports document the claim, not independent proof of a breach.

Alleged PwC Data Breach

The supplied leak-site screenshot names a directory, pwc-stg.csod.com, and describes Cornerstone OnDemand platform materials, regional HR exports, e-learning courses, and integration testing documents. It lists 494 directories, alongside 1,333 original archive containers and 53 nested containers. The screenshot alone does not establish how these materials were obtained.

Hackmanac reported that the alleged data spans PwC operations in Australia, China, Canada, and the UK. One HR dataset reportedly contains 213,084 records. That figure should not be read as a confirmed count of affected employees because the number of unique people remains unknown.

The alert also mentions employee information, employment and training records, internal audit methods, confidential documents, and single sign-on source code and configuration files. It does not establish whether working passwords, tokens, or other usable secrets are present.

The screenshot threatens publication after a countdown and urges the company to make contact. A reported October 28 release deadline has not been independently confirmed. No ransom amount, initial access method, or evidence of encrypted PwC systems has been established in the reviewed material.

Everest has previously used data theft claims to pressure named organizations, including its alleged McDonald’s India breach. However, its history includes both data extortion and file encryption, so this listing should not automatically be treated as proof of ransomware deployment.

A separate technical analysis of Everest ransomware found no data theft function inside one examined encryptor. Researchers noted that any theft could instead occur earlier through separate tools. That finding does not explain this alleged incident.
